directions.title: Isolating the Critical Bonding Energy Threshold for Thermal Crossover via Isotopic Ablation and High-Power-Density Phonon Perturbation
directions.abstract: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance is governed by the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length. We replace dynamic feedback control with direct materials-level perturbation, using isotopically purified references to minimize bulk isotope scattering and pulsed laser loading to induce non-equilibrium phonon populations. This structural substitution isolates the interfacial crossover boundary, establishing the quantitative validity limit of the maximum transmission limit model for weakly bonded interfaces by tracking the shift in the crossover length scale under high-power-density conditions, while explicitly decoupling bulk phonon mean free path reduction from interfacial structural degradation and phonon transmission bottlenecks.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable crossover length scale determined by the interface bonding energy and bulk phonon mean free path. Under high-power-density conditions, this crossover length scale shifts strictly due to the reduction of the bulk phonon mean free path caused by non-equilibrium phonon anharmonic scattering, while the intrinsic interface bonding energy and interfacial phonon transmission probability remain constant.

scientific_object.description: phononic_heterostructure_system with isotopically purified reference and sub-threshold pulsed excitation

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Non-equilibrium phonon population effects induced by high-power-density perturbation reduce the bulk phonon mean free path via enhanced anharmonic scattering, thereby shifting the crossover length scale where interface resistance dominates, relative to the fixed intrinsic interface bonding energy and transmission probability.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Substitution of the bulk material with an isotopically purified reference to minimize isotope scattering, combined with high-power-density, sub-threshold pulsed laser perturbation to induce non-equilibrium phonon populations without inducing interfacial structural degradation.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Isotopic purification minimizes bulk isotope scattering, allowing the interfacial Kapitza resistance to be isolated. High-power-density, sub-threshold perturbation populates non-equilibrium optical phonons, which increases bulk anharmonic scattering rates and reduces the effective bulk phonon mean free path, shifting the length scale at which interface resistance dominates, without altering the interface structure or creating high-frequency phonon transmission bottlenecks.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparison of the transient thermal decay curves between the standard heterostructure and the isotopically purified reference under identical high-power-density pulsing, combined with time-resolved phonon spectroscopy to verify that the shift in crossover length scale correlates with bulk optical phonon population decay rather than interfacial structural changes or high-frequency phonon reflection.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Quantitative extraction of the crossover length scale from transient thermal transport metrology, demonstrating a predictable shift correlated with bulk phonon MFP reduction (verified via time-resolved phonon spectroscopy) and decoupled from interfacial structural degradation or transmission bottlenecks.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Transient thermal transport metrology comparing isotopically purified references against standard heterostructures under high-power-density, sub-threshold pulsed laser loading, supplemented by time-resolved phonon spectroscopy.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim fails if the crossover length scale shifts unpredictably due to irreversible interface reconstruction under high power density, if the shift is driven by a non-equilibrium phonon transmission bottleneck at the interface rather than bulk anharmonic scattering, or if the mechanism does not apply to interfaces dominated purely by acoustic phonon scattering (e.g., weak van der Waals junctions).
hypothesis.claim_scope: Valid for phononic heterostructures with overlapping optical and acoustic phonon density of states under ultrafast, sub-threshold pulsed thermal loading where interfacial structural degradation is strictly avoided; invalid for purely acoustic van der Waals interfaces, steady-state low-flux conditions, or regimes where electronic heat conduction dominates.
assumptions: Isotopic purification effectively minimizes bulk isotope scattering without altering interfacial bonding topology.
Ultrafast pulsed loading induces non-equilibrium phonon populations before irreversible structural degradation occurs.
The ultrafast pulse duration and fluence are strictly bounded to prevent interfacial melting or reconstruction.
The non-equilibrium phonon population decays primarily via bulk anharmonic scattering rather than interfacial reflection or transmission bottlenecks.

directions.falsifier: Demonstration that the crossover length scale shift is entirely decoupled from bulk phonon mean free path reduction, or that it is driven by interfacial structural degradation, interfacial phonon transmission bottlenecks, or electronic thermal conduction.
directions.gap_alignment: The isotopic purification and high-power-density perturbation directly isolate the boundary variable (crossover length scale) and define the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit model for weakly bonded interfaces under non-equilibrium conditions, while controlling for interfacial degradation confounders.

trace.target_claim: The critical interface bonding energy threshold marking the crossover to interface-dominated thermal resistance can be isolated and quantified by physically ablating bulk scattering via isotopic purification and directly perturbing the phonon population with high-power-density pulses, defining the validity boundary of the maximum transmission limit model.
trace.scientific_concern: The candidate incorrectly claims that isotopic purification 'ablates bulk Umklapp scattering.' Isotopic purification only reduces mass-disorder (isotope) scattering; Umklapp scattering is an intrinsic anharmonic process. Furthermore, the 'critical interface bonding energy threshold' is an intrinsic material property of the interface and does not 'shift' under high power density. What shifts is the crossover length scale or the relative dominance of interface vs. bulk resistance due to the reduction of the bulk phonon mean free path under non-equilibrium conditions.
trace.opponent_concern: The conflation of intrinsic interface properties (bonding energy) with state-dependent transport properties (phonon mean free path) undermines the physical basis of the 'shifting threshold' claim, as bonding energy is a fixed chemical property of the interface.
trace.required_revision: Revise the mechanism to state that isotopic purification reduces isotope scattering (not Umklapp) to isolate interfacial resistance. Clarify that the intrinsic bonding energy threshold does not shift; rather, the crossover length scale or the relative dominance of interface resistance shifts due to the reduction of the bulk phonon mean free path under non-equilibrium high-power-density conditions.
alternative_explanations: The observed shift in thermal crossover under high power density may simply be due to bulk thermal conductivity degradation from increased anharmonic (Umklapp) scattering in the non-equilibrium state, rather than a fundamental shift in the interface's bonding energy threshold.
trace.final_scope: Valid for phononic heterostructures where isotopic purification effectively isolates interfacial resistance by minimizing bulk isotope scattering; the claim applies to the shift in the crossover length scale under non-equilibrium phonon populations, not a shift in the intrinsic interface bonding energy.

trace.opponent_concern: Localized interfacial heating or non-equilibrium phonon transmission bottlenecks at the interface could mimic the expected shift in the crossover length scale, confounding the attribution to bulk phonon mean free path reduction.

mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

directions.title: Feedback-Stabilized Mode-Resolved Phonon Invariant for Partitioning Heat Conduction in High-Power-Density Materials
directions.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials are conventionally partitioned using the macroscopic Wiedemann-Franz law, which fails under strong electron-phonon coupling. We replace this weak macroscopic partitioning with a closed-loop stabilized mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant, restricted to decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes. By applying controlled carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon pumping perturbations to a doped wide-bandgap semiconductor, we use ultrafast spectral phonon imaging to track the mode-resolved phonon mean free path distribution. A feedback loop adjusts the perturbation trajectory to maintain this phonon population invariant, effectively freezing the targeted optical phonon contribution. To address the confounding risk of perturbation-induced acoustic phonon scattering, the invariant maintenance is strictly bounded to regimes where the dominant heat-carrying acoustic phonon population remains invariant or is independently quantifiable. This enables the direct isolation of the electron thermal conductivity. Ablation against open-loop perturbation and stress testing near the thermal damage threshold confirm the identifiability of the partition and bound the validity domain where macroscopic laws fail.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation can be discriminated by maintaining a mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant for decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes via closed-loop feedback of carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon pumping perturbations, provided that the perturbation-induced alterations to the dominant acoustic phonon heat conduction are negligible or independently quantifiable, thereby structurally freezing the targeted optical phonon contribution and isolating the electron thermal conductivity.

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Feedback-stabilized mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant isolates electron heat conduction by structurally freezing targeted high-frequency optical phonon transport pathways, bounded by the condition that perturbation-induced changes to acoustic phonon scattering and transport are negligible or independently subtracted, bypassing non-linear electron-phonon scattering cascades.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Alter the carrier density and temperature via electrostatic gating and resistive heating, and apply coherent THz phonon pumping, while applying closed-loop feedback based on mode-resolved phonon mean free path deviations to maintain the phonon population invariant for decoupled high-frequency optical modes, concurrently monitoring and bounding the acoustic phonon mean free path distribution to ensure it remains unperturbed or independently quantifiable.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: By actively adjusting the perturbation trajectory, including coherent THz pumping, to freeze the mode-resolved phonon mean free path distribution of decoupled optical modes while ensuring the acoustic phonon population remains invariant, the optical phonon thermal conductivity contribution is held constant. Any subsequent changes in total thermal conductivity, after subtracting any bounded acoustic phonon variations, can then be directly attributed to the electron heat conduction contribution, bypassing the breakdown of the macroscopic Wiedemann-Franz law.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparison of the partitioned thermal conductivity trajectories under closed-loop invariant maintenance versus open-loop perturbation, demonstrating that only the closed-loop approach successfully isolates the electron contribution without concurrent optical or acoustic phonon scattering artifacts, confirmed by the invariance of the acoustic phonon mean free path distribution.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of the mode-resolved phonon mean free path distribution for decoupled optical modes remaining invariant under perturbation, concurrent verification that the acoustic phonon mean free path distribution remains invariant or is independently quantifiable, and the corresponding isolation of the electron thermal conductivity contribution, contrasted against the failure of open-loop perturbation to achieve the same separation.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of mode-resolved phonon MFP invariance for decoupled optical modes and bounded acoustic phonon perturbation under closed-loop perturbation, contrasted with open-loop ablation and bounded by thermal damage stress testing.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds only within the validity domain where the feedback loop can maintain the optical phonon invariant without inducing structural degradation, exceeding the thermal damage threshold, or significantly perturbing the dominant acoustic phonon modes; it fails when Joule heating gradients exceed the spatial resolution of the spectral phonon imaging, when latency prevents real-time correction, or when the perturbations inevitably alter the acoustic phonon mean free path beyond independent quantification.
hypothesis.claim_scope: High-power-density wide-bandgap semiconductors under controlled carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon perturbations, restricted to the validity domain of decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes, and strictly bounded to regimes where perturbation-induced alterations to the dominant acoustic phonon heat conduction are negligible or independently quantifiable.
assumptions: Mode-resolved phonon mean free path distributions can be accurately extracted via ultrafast X-ray diffraction and that high-frequency optical phonons can be spectrally separated from electronic excitations.
Decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes exist within the targeted wide-bandgap semiconductor whose scattering phase space is minimally affected by carrier density perturbations.

The dominant heat-carrying acoustic phonon modes can be spectrally and temporally resolved to verify their invariance, or their perturbation can be independently modeled and subtracted without introducing unquantifiable uncertainty into the electron thermal conductivity isolation.

directions.falsifier: Demonstration that phonon and electron contributions cannot be independently varied or measured with sufficient precision to distinguish their relative contributions, that Wiedemann-Franz deviations are dominated by mechanisms other than electron-phonon coupling, that no decoupled high-frequency optical modes exist in the material, or that the required perturbations inevitably and unquantifiably alter the dominant acoustic phonon heat conduction.
directions.gap_alignment: The feedback-stabilized invariant directly provides the missing discriminating observation and candidate mechanism, while the stress protocol, restriction to decoupled optical modes, and explicit bounding of acoustic phonon perturbations resolve the missing boundary condition and mitigate non-linear scattering cascades and confounding acoustic phonon alterations.

trace.target_claim: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation can be discriminated by maintaining a mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant via closed-loop feedback of carrier density and temperature perturbations, thereby structurally freezing the phonon contribution and isolating the electron thermal conductivity.
trace.scientific_concern: The assumption that macroscopic feedback of carrier density and temperature can maintain a mode-resolved phonon population invariant ignores non-linear electron-phonon scattering cascades. Altering carrier density inherently changes the electron-phonon scattering phase space, which non-linearly alters phonon lifetimes and mean free paths. Electrostatic gating and resistive heating lack the independent degrees of freedom required to suppress these cascades and freeze the phonon mean free path distribution.
trace.opponent_concern: The proposed feedback loop is physically under-actuated; tuning carrier density and temperature cannot independently control the phonon mean free path distribution because electron-phonon coupling intrinsically links them, meaning the 'invariant' cannot be maintained without triggering the very scattering cascades the method seeks to bypass.
trace.required_revision: Restrict the phonon population invariant to a specific subset of decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes where electron-phonon cascades are negligible, and introduce coherent THz phonon pumping as an additional actuation degree of freedom in the feedback loop to actively compensate for residual scattering changes.
alternative_explanations: The observed isolation of electron thermal conductivity could be an artifact of incomplete thermalization rather than a true decoupling of phonon and electron contributions, as the high-frequency optical modes may not be representative of the total phonon heat capacity.
trace.final_scope: High-power-density wide-bandgap semiconductors under controlled carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon perturbations, restricted to the validity domain of decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes.

trace.target_claim: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation can be discriminated by maintaining a mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant for decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes via closed-loop feedback of carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon pumping perturbations, thereby structurally freezing the targeted phonon contribution and isolating the electron thermal conductivity.
trace.scientific_concern: The perturbations used to freeze the optical phonons may simultaneously alter the population or mean free path of the dominant heat-carrying acoustic phonons via changes in phonon-phonon or electron-acoustic phonon scattering, meaning the observed change in total thermal conductivity is not solely due to the isolated electron contribution.
trace.opponent_concern: A competing mechanism or confounder could explain the same observation: the high-power perturbations (THz pumping, gating) may inadvertently perturb the dominant acoustic phonon modes or introduce localized Joule heating, confounding the isolation of the electron thermal conductivity.
trace.required_revision: Explicitly bound the claim to regimes where perturbation-induced changes to acoustic phonon transport are negligible or independently measurable, and incorporate acoustic phonon monitoring into the feedback loop or boundary conditions.
alternative_explanations: The perturbations used to freeze the optical phonons may simultaneously alter the population or mean free path of the dominant heat-carrying acoustic phonons via changes in phonon-phonon (Umklapp) or electron-acoustic phonon scattering, meaning the observed change in total thermal conductivity includes a perturbed acoustic phonon contribution rather than solely the isolated electron contribution.

Localized Joule heating or non-equilibrium hot carrier distributions from the high-power THz pumping and electrostatic gating may alter the local temperature gradient, confounding the extraction of the intrinsic electron thermal conductivity.
trace.final_scope: High-power-density wide-bandgap semiconductors under controlled carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon perturbations, restricted to the validity domain of decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes, and strictly bounded to regimes where perturbation-induced alterations to the dominant acoustic phonon heat conduction are negligible or independently quantifiable.

mature_idea.scientific_object: Twisted multilayer van der Waals heterostructures (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) with controlled interlayer rotation angles
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

mature_idea.mechanism: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. directions.title: Moiré-Pinning Thresholds Govern Structural Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures Under Thermal Cycling
directions.abstract: Random interlayer rotations engineered to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures are assumed to passively survive operational thermal cycling. We replace this weak assumption with a refined mechanism: structural stability is strictly governed by a twist-angle-dependent moiré potential energy corrugation that pins rotational configurations only when the rotational barrier exceeds the thermal activation energy. By synthesizing WSe2/MoSe2, WSe2/MoTe2, and MoS2/MoTe2 heterostructures and subjecting them to sustained thermal cycling, we demonstrate that engineered anisotropy persists exclusively in systems above this moiré corrugation threshold. Ablation via open-loop thermal cycling controls confirms that without sufficient moiré pinning, rotational relaxation rapidly recovers cross-plane conductivity. Crucially, we rule out interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation as alternative drivers of this recovery. This establishes the material-dependent boundary conditions for twist-angle thermal anisotropy.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Random interlayer rotations engineered to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling only if the moiré potential energy corrugation exceeds the thermal activation energy, and the observed recovery of cross-plane thermal conductivity in unstable systems is strictly attributable to rotational relaxation rather than interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation.

scientific_object.description: random_interlayer_rotations and moiré potential energy corrugation in van der Waals heterostructures, bounded against interlayer atomic diffusion

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling, suppressing cross-plane conductance. The stability of this disorder under thermal stress is dictated by the moiré potential energy landscape; specifically, when the potential energy corrugation exceeds the thermal activation barrier, the engineered anisotropy persists. If the corrugation is insufficient, thermal fluctuations drive rotational relaxation, degrading the thermal bottleneck, provided no interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bonding occurs to artificially restore phonon coupling.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Replacement of the passive structural stability assumption with the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential energy corrugation as the governing mechanism, validated across diverse van der Waals heterostructures under sustained thermal cycling while explicitly ruling out interlayer chemical bonding.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: By explicitly bounding the stability claim to the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential energy corrugation and ruling out interlayer diffusion, the intervention ensures that the engineered cross-plane thermal conductivity suppression is maintained by a quantifiable rotational energy barrier rather than a passive assumption of kinetic trapping, total adhesion, or chemical bonding.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Observation of cross-plane thermal conductivity recovery to within 20% of pristine aligned values, correlated with the loss of in-situ Raman moiré superlattice signatures, specifically in material systems where the moiré potential corrugation falls below the thermal activation threshold, AND confirmed by cross-sectional STEM/EELS to show no interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Demonstration of rotational relaxation to equilibrium stacking within device-relevant thermal cycling conditions, resulting in the recovery of cross-plane thermal conductivity to within 20% of pristine aligned values, correlated with the loss of in-situ Raman moiré superlattice signatures, in the confirmed absence of interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bonding.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements of cross-plane thermal conductivity, in-situ Raman spectroscopy of moiré superlattice peak positions and linewidths during sustained thermal cycling, and cross-sectional STEM/EELS to verify the absence of interlayer diffusion.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds when the moiré potential energy corrugation exceeds the thermal activation energy at operational temperatures (e.g., 300 K to 500 K) and interlayer diffusion is negligible. It fails when the corrugation falls below this threshold, causing irreversible relaxation to equilibrium stacking and recovery of cross-plane conductivity, OR if interlayer diffusion/covalent bonding occurs and artificially recovers conductivity regardless of the moiré barrier.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Applicable to van der Waals heterostructures (e.g., WSe2/MoSe2, WSe2/MoTe2, MoS2/MoTe2) where the moiré potential energy corrugation and rotational barrier can be independently tuned via twist angle and material selection, provided operational temperatures remain below the threshold for interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation.
assumptions: In-situ Raman moiré superlattice signatures are sufficiently sensitive to resolve rotational drift in real time.
Cross-plane thermal conductivity changes are primarily driven by rotational relaxation rather than changes in substrate properties or thermal contact resistance.
Operational thermal cycling temperatures (e.g., up to 500 K) are sufficiently low to prevent interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation across the van der Waals gap.

directions.falsifier: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking and recover cross-plane conductivity even when the moiré potential corrugation is theoretically above the thermal activation threshold, OR demonstration that the recovery of conductivity is accompanied by interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation rather than pure rotational relaxation.
directions.gap_alignment: Addresses the material generality boundary condition by extending the mechanism to diverse TMD heterostructures, and resolves the missing assumption of operational stability by defining the moiré potential corrugation threshold as the governing physical invariant, while explicitly bounding against chemical confounders.

trace.target_claim: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered cross-plane thermal conductivity suppression in van der Waals heterostructures is strictly bounded by a twist-angle-dependent moiré potential energy threshold that must exceed the thermal activation barrier for rotational relaxation.
trace.scientific_concern: The candidate conflates total interlayer binding energy with the moiré potential energy corrugation. Structural pinning against rotational relaxation is governed by the potential energy barrier (corrugation) between metastable states, not the total adhesion energy. High binding energy with low corrugation would not prevent relaxation.
trace.opponent_concern: The total interlayer binding energy does not strictly dictate rotational stability; it is the energy barrier (corrugation) of the moiré potential landscape that must exceed the thermal activation energy. Without this distinction, the hypothesis fails to account for interfaces with high adhesion but low rotational barriers.
trace.required_revision: Revise the mechanism and hypothesis to specify that the moiré pinning threshold is defined by the moiré potential energy corrugation (barrier height for rotational relaxation) exceeding the thermal activation energy, rather than the total interlayer binding energy.
alternative_explanations: Rotational relaxation could be driven by localized defect-mediated slip rather than uniform thermal activation over the moiré potential barrier.
Cross-plane thermal conductivity recovery could be caused by interfacial delamination or void formation rather than intrinsic rotational relaxation.
trace.final_scope: Applicable to van der Waals heterostructures where the moiré potential energy corrugation and rotational barrier can be tuned via twist angle and material selection, provided that structural relaxation is the primary driver of thermal conductivity changes.

directions.title: Direct Observation of Thermal Transport Limits via Thermally-Driven Twist-Angle Relaxation in Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Multilayers
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat transfer in twisted van der Waals multilayers are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the structural stability of twist-angle-engineered interfaces under high power density remains unobserved. We replace the assumption of a static interfacial phonon scattering landscape with a refined mechanism of thermally-activated twist-angle relaxation, which structurally reconstructs the moiré superlattice and modulates thermal transport. By applying time-domain thermoreflectance measurements before and after high-power thermal cycling, we directly observe the thermal saturation phenomenon and isolate the structural scattering mechanism, explicitly ruling out confounders such as hot-phonon bottlenecking and irreversible defect generation. Ablation across varying transition metal dichalcogenide multilayers validates the structural stability boundary condition and material generality, quantifying coherent twist-angle distribution changes via electron diffraction and critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Thermally-activated twist-angle relaxation structurally reconstructs the moiré superlattice, modulating interfacial phonon scattering and imposing a fundamental upper bound on cross-plane interfacial thermal resistance under high power density, provided that thermal flux remains below the threshold for irreversible defect generation and hot-phonon bottlenecking.

trace.target_claim: Thermally-driven twist-angle relaxation dynamically alters the moiré superlattice, imposing a fundamental upper bound on cross-plane interfacial thermal resistance under high power density.
trace.scientific_concern: The candidate conflates the heat transfer mechanism (interfacial phonon scattering) with a structural instability mechanism (thermally-activated twist-angle relaxation). Twist-angle relaxation does not replace phonon scattering; rather, it represents a structural boundary condition that modulates the phonon scattering landscape under high thermal loads. Additionally, describing relaxation as 'dynamically altering' implies reversible fluctuations, whereas relaxation is typically an irreversible or metastable structural transition.
trace.opponent_concern: Twist-angle relaxation in van der Waals multilayers typically requires temperatures approaching the material's thermal degradation limit or specific sliding mechanisms that may not be purely thermally activated at the operational power densities of interest, potentially confounding the attribution of thermal resistance changes to pure twist-angle relaxation versus general thermal degradation or interlayer sliding.
trace.required_revision: Clarify that twist-angle relaxation is a structural instability that modulates (rather than replaces) interfacial phonon scattering, and reframe 'dynamic' to 'thermally-activated' or 'metastable' to accurately reflect the structural nature of the relaxation.
alternative_explanations: Changes in interfacial thermal resistance under high power density may be driven by thermally induced interlayer sliding or defect generation rather than coherent twist-angle relaxation.

Thermal resistance saturation could be an artifact of hot phonon effects or measurement limitations in time-domain thermoreflectance at high temperature gradients, rather than a fundamental structural limit.
trace.final_scope: Limits of cross-plane thermal transport in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides under high power density, bounded by thermally-activated twist-angle relaxation and structural stability.

directions.title: Feedback-Bounded Thermal Cycling: In-Situ Characterization and MD-Validated Critical Binding Energy Thresholds for Twist-Angle Stability in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat transfer in twisted van der Waals heterostructures are constrained by the structural stability of the twist angle under high power density. We investigate the thermomechanical limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy by identifying the intrinsic critical binding energy threshold for interlayer sliding, which governs moiré phonon scattering and thermal saturation. By utilizing in-situ thermal and structural characterization during controlled thermal cycling, we precisely bound this threshold and isolate the phonon scattering boundaries prior to catastrophic delamination, while explicitly decoupling these effects from point defect generation and intrinsic Umklapp scattering. By measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity, twist angle distribution, and defect concentrations before and after thermal cycling, we validate the stability assumption across MoS2/WS2 and extend it to other transition metal dichalcogenides, resolving the unmapped phenomena of thermal saturation and structural degradation at the nanoscale.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The structural stability and thermal transport limits of twisted transition metal dichalcogenides under high power density are intrinsically governed by a material-specific critical binding energy threshold for interlayer sliding, which dictates the onset of moiré phonon scattering and thermal saturation, provided that point defect generation (e.g., chalcogen vacancies) and intrinsic Umklapp scattering limits are decoupled via in-situ thermal and structural characterization during controlled thermal cycling.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: As thermal load increases, the system approaches the intrinsic critical binding energy threshold for interlayer sliding; crossing this threshold induces structural sliding that alters the moiré superlattice, thereby modifying phonon scattering pathways and causing thermal saturation. This mechanism is distinct from and can be decoupled from thermal saturation driven by point defect generation or intrinsic Umklapp scattering limits.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparing the thermal conductivity and twist-angle distribution evolution during controlled thermal cycling against molecular dynamics predictions, while simultaneously monitoring chalcogen vacancy concentrations (e.g., via photoluminescence or Raman spectroscopy) and electron-phonon coupling rates, to observe whether thermal saturation and structural degradation onset precisely at the predicted critical binding energy threshold for sliding, distinguishing it from defect-mediated or intrinsic scattering mechanisms.

directions.title: Structural Stability Limits of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: The assumption that twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy remains structurally stable under high power density is a critical bottleneck in predicting thermal transport limits in nanoscale devices. We replace the static interfacial thermal resistance model with a dynamic phonon-moiré scattering and interfacial phonon transmission mechanism that accounts for twist-angle degradation, while explicitly isolating this effect from localized phase transitions and point defect generation. By subjecting twisted bilayer 2H-phase transition metal dichalcogenides (MoS2/WS2) to controlled thermal cycling below phase transition thresholds, we directly observe the cross-plane thermal conductivity limits and quantify twist-angle distribution changes via nanobeam electron diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. This approach isolates the structural stability boundary condition, providing a direct observation of thermal transport saturation and resolving the evidence deficit in atomic-scale interfacial bonding metrology.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The thermal transport limit and interfacial thermal resistance in twist-angle-engineered semiconducting TMDs are fundamentally bounded by the structural stability of the moiré superlattice under high power density, which dynamically alters phonon-moiré scattering and interfacial phonon transmission, provided that localized phase transitions and point defect generation are strictly excluded.

scientific_object.description: twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides (e.g., MoS2/WS2) in the 2H phase, subjected to high power density thermal cycling below phase transition and defect generation thresholds

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Joint mechanism linking dynamic phonon-moiré scattering and interfacial phonon transmission to twist-angle relaxation, isolated from phase transition and defect scattering.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Subjecting the twisted 2H-phase TMD interfaces to controlled thermal cycling below the phase transition threshold to perturb the structural stability, and comparing the cross-plane thermal conductivity and twist-angle distribution before and after perturbation.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Thermal cycling below phase transition thresholds induces twist-angle relaxation and interfacial strain, which alters the moiré superlattice periodicity and interfacial phonon transmission, thereby shifting the thermal transport limit and increasing interfacial thermal resistance beyond the static geometric prediction without triggering 2H-to-1T transitions.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Direct measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity combined with nanobeam electron diffraction and Raman spectroscopy to simultaneously quantify twist-angle distribution changes and verify the absence of localized phase transitions or point defects.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Quantitative comparison of cross-plane thermal conductivity, twist-angle distribution, and phase purity before and after thermal cycling, validated against molecular dynamics simulations of critical binding energy thresholds and phonon density of states.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of thermal transport saturation and structural degradation in nanoscale electronic materials under high power density, contrasting pristine and thermally cycled states while verifying phase stability.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds strictly as long as the thermal cycling remains below the critical binding energy threshold for irreversible interfacial delamination, below the threshold for significant point defect generation, and below the critical temperature for localized 2H-to-1T phase transitions; beyond these thresholds, macroscopic delamination, defect scattering, or phase-boundary scattering dominates.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Valid for twist-angle-engineered 2H-phase semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenide interfaces under high power density thermal loading, bounded by the critical binding energy threshold for structural stability, the threshold for point defect generation, and the phase transition temperature, where phonon-moiré scattering dominates.
assumptions: Assumes that thermal cycling primarily induces moiré-scale twist-angle relaxation rather than phase transitions or defect generation, and that cross-plane phonon transport is the dominant bottleneck for heat dissipation in these specific nanoscale devices.

directions.falsifier: Evidence that twist-angle relaxation does not significantly alter the cross-plane phonon transmission compared to the baseline static model, or that observed thermal resistance changes are primarily driven by localized phase transitions or point defects rather than moiré scattering.

directions.title: Non-Equilibrium Hot-Phonon Spectroscopy Reveals Bonding-Dependent Thermal Boundary Resistance Limits at Epitaxial Metal-Dielectric Interfaces Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: Interfacial thermal resistance at metal-dielectric junctions limits heat dissipation in high-power-density nanoelectronics, yet the atomic-scale bonding configurations that minimize Kapitza resistance under non-equilibrium conditions remain unidentified. We replace linear-response phonon mapping with non-equilibrium hot-phonon spectroscopy within a closed-loop experimental framework to directly observe atomic-scale interfacial bonding and thermal transport. By coupling ultrafast electron diffraction and high-flux time-domain thermoreflectance with iterative plasma-mediated termination control of epitaxial TiN/MgO interfaces, we map the causal chain from atomic termination to thermal transport ceilings dominated by hot-phonon bottlenecks and slow anharmonic optical-to-acoustic decay, explicitly bounding the fluence to exclude transient defect generation. Ablation of the non-equilibrium spectroscopy module confirms that capturing non-linear phonon-phonon interactions, rather than linear-response approximations or structural disorder artifacts, is required to identify the true minimum-resistance bonding configuration. This resolves the evidence deficit in atomic-scale interfacial thermal metrology by providing direct, high-flux observation of the structure-property mechanism governing thermal boundary limits.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Non-equilibrium hot-phonon bottlenecks driven by slow anharmonic optical-to-acoustic phonon decay, rather than linear-response phonon transmission or transient structural disorder, dictate the fundamental lower bound of interfacial thermal resistance at epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces under high power density, provided pump fluence remains below the defect-generation threshold.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: High-flux pumping generates non-equilibrium optical phonon populations that accumulate at the interface because the anharmonic decay rate into acoustic phonons is slower than the acoustic phonon transmission rate across the interface, creating a hot-phonon bottleneck that linear-response models fail to capture, thereby setting the true thermal transport ceiling.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The ablation comparator using linear-response mapping will converge to a falsely low thermal boundary resistance, whereas the non-equilibrium spectroscopy will reveal the higher, physically accurate resistance floor caused by hot-phonon accumulation, with the difference scaling predictably with pump fluence below the defect-generation and damage thresholds, distinguishing it from resistance increases caused by transient disorder.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of non-equilibrium phonon dispersion and population decay at the interface via ultrafast electron diffraction, correlated with thermal boundary resistance measurements across varying fluences, compared against linear-response baselines and defect-generation thresholds.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Ultrafast electron diffraction and high-flux time-domain thermoreflectance measurements of non-equilibrium phonon populations at epitaxial TiN/MgO interfaces, bounded by strict fluence thresholds to prevent measurement artifacts and transient disorder.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds for epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces under high power density where optical phonon lifetimes exceed acoustic phonon transit times; it fails if the pump fluence exceeds the ablation, non-thermal melting, or defect-generation thresholds, or if the interface is entirely amorphous, masking coherent phonon transmission.

directions.title: Hot Phonon Bottleneck Saturation at Covalently Bonded Graphene-Diamond Interfaces: A Non-Equilibrium Thermal Transport Ceiling Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: Thermal transport at nanoscale interfaces is conventionally described by equilibrium boundary resistance, failing to predict dissipation limits under high power density. We propose that an interfacial hot phonon transmission bottleneck—distinct from the intrinsic hot phonon bottleneck, electron-phonon thermalization limit, and anharmonic scattering—creates a fundamental thermal ceiling where non-equilibrium optical phonons accumulate at the boundary faster than they transmit. Using graphene-on-diamond heterostructures with systematically varied covalent sp³ versus van der Waals bonding, we apply high-power perturbations to drive non-equilibrium conditions. Ultrafast thermal metrology measures the saturation heat flux, revealing that covalent bonding raises the thermal ceiling by opening transmission channels that prevent interfacial optical phonon pile-up. Stepwise annealing ablates bond density to isolate this non-equilibrium interfacial mechanism from intrinsic bulk phonon dynamics, electron-phonon coupling limits, and equilibrium defect scattering.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Under high power density, an interfacial hot phonon transmission bottleneck—distinct from the intrinsic hot phonon bottleneck within the graphene layer, the electron-phonon thermalization limit, and temperature-dependent anharmonic scattering—creates a thermal transport saturation ceiling governed by the pile-up of non-equilibrium optical phonons at the boundary due to density of states mismatch, which is tunable via covalent interfacial bonding.

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: interfacial_hot_phonon_transmission_bottleneck: non-equilibrium optical phonons accumulate at the material interface when their transmission rate into the adjacent material is limited by density of states mismatch and weak coupling, creating a thermal ceiling distinct from the intrinsic optical-to-acoustic phonon decay bottleneck, the electron-phonon thermalization limit, and anharmonic scattering, with the ceiling value scaling with interfacial covalent bond density.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Synthesizing graphene-on-diamond heterostructures with systematically varied covalent sp³ interfacial bonding, and applying calibrated high-power perturbations to drive non-equilibrium phonon populations while isolating interfacial effects from intrinsic bulk bottlenecks, electron-phonon limits, and anharmonic scattering.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Covalent sp³ bridges open phonon transmission channels and broaden the interfacial density of states, preventing optical phonon pile-up at the boundary and thereby raising the thermal transport ceiling compared to van der Waals interfaces where the interfacial hot phonon bottleneck saturates heat flux, independent of electron-phonon coupling rates.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparing the saturation heat flux and interfacial thermal resistance evolution measured via ultrafast thermal metrology across covalently bonded versus van der Waals interfaces, while explicitly decoupling the interfacial transmission ceiling from the intrinsic electron-phonon thermalization limit and temperature-dependent anharmonic scattering via ultrafast temporal discrimination or selective optical phonon excitation.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of an interfacial thermal transport ceiling (saturation heat flux) that shifts monotonically with interfacial covalent bond density, measured via precision thermal metrology under high power density perturbation, with explicit decoupling from intrinsic bulk bottlenecks, electron-phonon limits, and anharmonic scattering.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of interfacial thermal transport ceiling saturation at graphene-diamond interfaces under high power density, with comparative measurements across covalent and van der Waals bonding configurations demonstrating mechanism-dependent ceiling values, contingent on decoupling from electron-phonon and anharmonic confounders.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The interfacial hot phonon bottleneck mechanism fails to dominate if the electron-phonon thermalization time exceeds the interfacial phonon transmission time, if localized Joule heating induces strong anharmonic scattering that masks the transmission bottleneck, if the intrinsic hot phonon bottleneck within the graphene layer becomes the rate-limiting step, or if bulk defect scattering introduced during plasma treatment masks the interfacial transmission enhancement.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Nanoscale material interfaces (graphene-diamond heterostructures) under high power density (>1 TW/m²) where interfacial non-equilibrium optical phonon transmission limits dominate over intrinsic electron-phonon thermalization and temperature-dependent anharmonic scattering; not applicable to equilibrium low-power conditions or bulk thermal transport.
assumptions: Non-equilibrium optical phonon populations can be generated at achievable power densities; interfacial bond density can be systematically varied without introducing confounding defect scattering; ultrafast metrology can resolve the relevant interfacial phonon timescales (<10 ps) distinct from bulk relaxation and electron-phonon thermalization; the electron-phonon thermalization time is sufficiently fast or can be independently decoupled.

directions.falsifier: A result showing the thermal ceiling is entirely governed by the electron-phonon thermalization limit in graphene, by temperature-dependent anharmonic scattering, or by the intrinsic hot phonon bottleneck within the graphene layer regardless of interfacial bonding.

directions.title: Feedback-Guided Twist-Angle Modulation and In-Situ Annealing to Bound Moiré-Mediated Interfacial Thermal Resistance
directions.abstract: Heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics is bottlenecked by interfacial thermal boundary resistance, which classical spatially averaged models fail to predict at atomically sharp, twisted interfaces. We propose that interfacial phonon coupling, governed by the periodic moiré potential and local stacking registry, dictates cross-plane heat transfer when the lattice twist angle is precisely modulated in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers. By closing the loop between time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements and twist-angle modulation, we systematically tune the interfacial structural state to maximize phonon spectral overlap. We perform in-situ thermal annealing to ablate extrinsic defect and contaminant scattering, apply high-power-density optical pumping to stress-test fundamental thermal saturation limits, and utilize complementary phonon spectroscopy to decouple bulk and strain-induced effects. This work establishes the intrinsic limits of heat transfer at atomic-scale moiré interfaces under high power density, moving beyond classical diffuse mismatch approximations while rigorously bounding strain and bulk confounders.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance in twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers is fundamentally modulated by twist-angle-dependent local interfacial registry and phonon transmission mediated by the periodic moiré potential, distinct from twist-induced bulk phonon dispersion changes or local strain-field variations, extending beyond the spatially averaged predictions of classical diffuse acoustic mismatch scattering.

scientific_object.description: twisted MoSe2/WSe2 moiré superlattice with atomically sharp, clean van der Waals interface, with rigorously decoupled bulk and strain effects

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: moiré-mediated local interfacial registry and phonon transmission, decoupled from twist-induced strain and bulk phonon dispersion changes
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Deterministic twist-angle modulation guided by time-domain thermoreflectance readouts, combined with in-situ thermal annealing to remove extrinsic defects and contaminants, high-power-density optical stress testing, and complementary phonon spectroscopy to decouple bulk and strain effects.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Modulating the twist angle alters the moiré superlattice periodicity and the spatial distribution of local stacking registries (e.g., AA, AB), tuning the local interfacial bonding landscape and phonon transmission probability, which directly modulates the effective cross-plane phonon coupling and thus the interfacial thermal resistance, independent of twist-induced bulk phonon dispersion changes or local strain-field variations.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The interfacial thermal resistance exhibits a non-monotonic, periodic dependence on the twist angle that persists after in-situ annealing, correlates strictly with local stacking registry rather than global strain magnitude, and remains distinct from changes in bulk phonon dispersion or group velocity as verified by complementary Raman/photoluminescence spectroscopy.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Quantitative measurement of interfacial thermal resistance as a function of twist angle via TDTR with rigorous decoupling of bulk, transducer, and strain effects, comparison of as-exfoliated and annealed states to bound extrinsic scattering and contaminant trapping, and observation of thermal saturation thresholds under high-power optical pumping.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: TDTR measurements of interfacial thermal resistance across twist angles, comparison of as-exfoliated vs annealed states, high-power optical pumping stress tests, and complementary Raman/PL spectroscopy to verify bulk phonon dispersion stability.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds for atomically sharp, clean interfaces where the moiré period is comparable to or smaller than the dominant cross-plane phonon mean free path, and where TDTR modeling and complementary spectroscopy can rigorously decouple the moiré interface resistance from bulk, transducer, and strain-induced contributions; it fails when high power density induces irreversible interlayer sliding, delamination, or when extrinsic contamination, strain-induced phonon localization, or bulk dispersion changes dominate the thermal resistance.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Atomically sharp twisted transition metal dichalcogenide interfaces under high power density, where the moiré period is comparable to or smaller than the dominant cross-plane phonon mean free path, and where twist-induced local strain fields, bulk phonon dispersion perturbations, and extrinsic contaminant trapping are rigorously decoupled from the interfacial transmission effects.
assumptions: Extrinsic defect scattering and contaminant trapping can be sufficiently removed via in-situ annealing to reveal intrinsic moiré phonon effects.
TDTR modeling and complementary phonon spectroscopy can rigorously decouple the ultra-thin moiré interface thermal resistance from bulk, transducer, and strain-induced contributions.

The dominant cross-plane phonon wavelengths are comparable to or larger than the moiré period to enable coherent or registry-dependent transport effects, without being dominated by moiré-boundary phonon localization.

directions.falsifier: A result showing the twist-angle dependence of thermal resistance is fully explained by twist-induced local strain fields altering bulk phonon dispersion, by phonon localization at moiré boundaries, by twist-angle-dependent trapping of extrinsic contaminants, or that the measured changes are dominated by extrinsic transducer interface variations rather than the moiré interface.

trace.target_claim: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance in twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers is fundamentally governed by twist-angle-dependent interfacial phonon coupling mediated by the periodic moiré potential, rather than classical diffusive acoustic mismatch scattering.
trace.scientific_concern: The claim that moiré-mediated phonon coupling entirely replaces classical acoustic mismatch scattering is overly absolute; at room temperature, inelastic scattering and diffusive transport still play critical roles, and the moiré potential primarily modulates the local interfacial registry and phonon transmission probability rather than replacing the underlying scattering physics. Additionally, isolating the single-interface moiré resistance via TDTR requires rigorous decoupling from bulk and transducer interface resistances.
trace.opponent_concern: At room temperature, the dominant phonon wavelengths (~1-2 nm) may be smaller than the moiré period for most twist angles, reducing the effect to a simple spatial average of local stacking registries (e.g., AA vs. AB) rather than true moiré-potential-driven coherent transport. Furthermore, TDTR may lack the sensitivity to isolate the intrinsic moiré interface resistance from the dominant transducer-TMD and bulk TMD thermal resistances.
trace.required_revision: Soften the claim from 'replacing classical diffusive acoustic mismatch scattering' to 'modulating local interfacial registry and phonon transmission beyond spatially averaged classical mismatch models', and explicitly acknowledge the TDTR decoupling challenge in the boundary conditions.
alternative_explanations: The observed twist-angle dependence in thermal resistance is merely a macroscopic spatial average of varying local stacking registries (e.g., fraction of AA vs. AB stacking) rather than a coherent moiré-potential-mediated phonon transport phenomenon.
The measured thermal resistance changes are dominated by extrinsic variations in the top transducer interface or bulk TMD defects rather than the bottom moiré interface.
trace.final_scope: Atomically sharp twisted transition metal dichalcogenide interfaces under high power density, where the moiré period is comparable to or smaller than the dominant cross-plane phonon mean free path, and where TDTR modeling can rigorously decouple the moiré interface resistance from bulk and transducer contributions.

trace.target_claim: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance in twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers is fundamentally modulated by twist-angle-dependent local interfacial registry and phonon transmission mediated by the periodic moiré potential, extending beyond the spatially averaged predictions of classical diffuse acoustic mismatch scattering.
trace.opponent_concern: A competing mechanism or confounder could explain the same observation: the observed twist-angle dependence of thermal resistance could be driven by twist-induced local strain fields altering bulk phonon dispersion, phonon localization at moiré boundaries, or twist-angle-dependent trapping of extrinsic contaminants, rather than solely by moiré-mediated interfacial registry and phonon transmission.
trace.required_revision: Explicitly bound the central hypothesis and claim scope to distinguish moiré-mediated interfacial phonon transmission from twist-induced bulk phonon dispersion changes, local strain-field variations, and extrinsic contaminant trapping.
alternative_explanations: Twist-induced local strain fields and interlayer distance variations altering the intrinsic phonon dispersion and group velocities within the layers.
Phonon localization or Umklapp-like scattering at the moiré superlattice boundaries reducing cross-plane transport.
Twist-angle-dependent trapping of extrinsic contaminants (e.g., polymer residues) in local strain minima acting as thermal barriers.

directions.title: Spectral Thermal Boundary Conductance Calibration via Phonon Spectroscopy Feedback in van der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet kinetic transport models rely on static boundary assumptions that fail to predict when interface resistance overtakes bulk resistance. We replace the static Kapitza resistance assumption with a dynamically calibrated spectral thermal boundary conductance, driven by iterative model-experiment calibration using mean-free-path-resolving phonon spectroscopy in dielectric-dielectric systems. By closing the loop between time-domain thermoreflectance measurements and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation via inverse modeling, we establish the exact physical and power-density thresholds where interfacial resistance dominates, explicitly decoupling phonon spectral mismatch from electron-phonon and defect-scattering confounders. This mechanism-commit innovation resolves the unmapped boundary variable gap, enabling predictive thermal design for high-power-density electronics.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Dynamically calibrating the spectral thermal boundary conductance via iterative inverse modeling of mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy data in dielectric-dielectric van der Waals heterostructures will accurately predict the power-density threshold where interfacial thermal resistance overtakes bulk thermal resistance, outperforming static boundary assumptions by isolating phonon spectral mismatch from electron-phonon and defect-scattering confounders.

scientific_object.description: atomically sharp dielectric-dielectric van der Waals heterostructure interface in nanoscale electronic devices

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Spectral phonon transmission mismatch at atomically sharp dielectric-dielectric interfaces governs the crossover from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance, and this crossover point is predictable only when the interfacial boundary variable is dynamically calibrated against mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy measurements, free from electron-phonon non-equilibrium and defect-scattering confounders.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Replacing the static Kapitza resistance boundary condition in the phonon Boltzmann transport equation with a dynamically updated spectral thermal boundary conductance driven by inverse modeling of mean-free-path-resolving phonon spectroscopy measurements, specifically decoupled from electron-phonon and defect-scattering artifacts.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Iterative refinement of the interfacial boundary variable in the Boltzmann transport equation, constrained by mode-specific phonon scattering rates and spectral transmission measurements in dielectric-dielectric systems, allows the kinetic transport model to accurately capture the onset of non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations that cause interface resistance to dominate bulk conduction, without convolution from metallic electron-phonon dynamics.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparison of total thermal resistance predictions between the inversely calibrated model and the bulk conduction ablation under high power density stress in dielectric-dielectric heterostructures, isolating the divergence point where interfacial resistance dominates, while using variable modulation frequencies to decouple thermal penetration depth from interfacial defect scattering.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Mode-specific phonon group velocities and spectral transmission measurements at the dielectric-dielectric heterostructure interface across multiple thermal penetration depths, contrasted against total thermal resistance predictions under varying power densities, with explicit decoupling of defect-scattering contributions.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy measurements (TDTR/FDTR) of interfacial phonon dynamics in dielectric-dielectric systems correlated with total thermal resistance measurements across power-density sweeps, demonstrating convergence of the calibrated spectral thermal boundary conductance and correct prediction of the bulk-to-interface resistance crossover.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The model's validity boundary is reached when high power density stress induces dominant non-linear three-phonon Umklapp scattering, when interfacial defect density exceeds the threshold for defect-dominated scattering, or when non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations diverge the calibrated boundary variable.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Atomically sharp dielectric-dielectric van der Waals heterostructures under moderate power densities where quasi-equilibrium phonon distributions hold at the interface and interfacial defect densities are low; excludes regimes with dominant non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations, strong anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering, metallic transducer electron-phonon non-equilibrium, and high defect densities.
assumptions: Quasi-equilibrium phonon distributions at the dielectric-dielectric interface under moderate power density; linear boundary conductance assumption holds when hot optical phonon populations remain below non-equilibrium threshold; phonon spectroscopy can resolve mode-specific interfacial scattering with sufficient signal-to-noise ratio; interfacial defect density is low enough that defect-mediated scattering does not dominate the spectral transmission mismatch.

directions.falsifier: A result showing the stated gap is resolved without this hypothesis, that the inversely calibrated boundary variable fails to improve predictive accuracy over static assumptions across the targeted power-density range, or that the observed resistance divergence is primarily driven by interfacial defects or electron-phonon non-equilibrium rather than spectral phonon transmission mismatch.

directions.title: Bounding Adaptive Cross-Plane Thermal Conductivity in Twisted TMDs via Strain-Mediated Interlayer Registry Modulation
directions.abstract: Dynamic modulation of cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted van der Waals heterostructures is often assumed to arise purely from affine moiré potential changes under strain. We replace this assumption with a refined mechanism of strain-induced local moiré superlattice reconstruction and interlayer registry modulation, where cross-plane thermal transport is governed by the formation and motion of strain solitons. Crucially, we explicitly decouple this mechanism from confounding out-of-plane van der Waals gap expansion (Poisson effect) and intralayer phonon dispersion shifts. By quantifying local registry changes via ultrafast electron diffraction and independently bounding out-of-plane lattice spacing, we establish the structural stability boundary conditions for adaptive thermal management. directions.title: Thermally Activated Interfacial Shear Creep and Stability Boundaries in Twist-Angle-Engineered van der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered van der Waals heterostructures offer tunable thermal transport, but their operational limits are constrained by structural relaxation under thermal load. Moving beyond classical bulk phase transformation kinetics, we identify thermally activated interfacial shear creep mediated by moiré domain wall (soliton) glide as the fundamental mechanism governing twist-angle stability, provided interfacial delamination and chemical degradation are negligible. By applying controlled isothermal annealing and thermal cycling to MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides, we map the critical temperature-time boundaries where interfacial soliton glide initiates. Electron diffraction and cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements validate the structural and thermal degradation, while molecular dynamics determine the critical Peierls-like energy thresholds for domain wall motion. This establishes a predictive creep-based stability boundary for high-power-density thermal management, explicitly distinguishing soliton glide from point-defect slip and thermal expansion-induced delamination.

assumptions: Moiré domain walls exhibit a well-defined Peierls-like energy barrier for glide; molecular dynamics can accurately capture the activation energy for soliton motion at relevant timescales; nanobeam electron diffraction can resolve domain wall glide without inducing beam damage; interfacial chemical stability is maintained during the thermal protocol.

mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

directions.title: Quantitative Crossover Boundary from Bulk-Dominated to Interface-Dominated Thermal Resistance in Heterogeneous Interfaces Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable critical interface transmission threshold that scales with the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length. This threshold shifts under high-power-density conditions due to non-equilibrium phonon-phonon scattering altering effective bulk transport lengths and specific mode-coupling at the interface, provided that electron-phonon decoupling and irreversible structural degradation are sub-dominant.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable critical spectrally resolved interface transmission threshold that scales with the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length. Under high-power-density conditions, this threshold shifts due to non-equilibrium phonon-phonon scattering altering effective bulk transport lengths and specific mode-coupling at the interface, assuming the regime is bounded such that electron-phonon non-equilibrium and irreversible structural degradation do not dominate the thermal response.

scientific_object.description: Heterogeneous material interfaces (metal-semiconductor, dielectric-substrate, van der Waals junctions) with systematically varied bonding topology, contamination levels, and chemical heterogeneity, operated within thermal and electrical regimes where lattice phonon scattering dominates over electron-phonon decoupling.

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering and interfacial Kapitza resistance. The crossover point depends on the bulk phonon mean free path distribution and the spectrally resolved interface transmission probability. Under high heat flux, non-equilibrium phonon-phonon scattering alters the effective bulk mean free path and modifies specific phonon mode-coupling at the interface, shifting the crossover threshold, provided electron-phonon coupling remains in equilibrium and the interface structure remains reversible.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Systematically alter interface bonding topology and contamination levels to map the spectrally resolved interface transmission function, and perturb the system with high power density to induce non-equilibrium phonon populations, while maintaining conditions below the threshold for irreversible structural degradation and significant electron-phonon decoupling.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Non-equilibrium phonon-phonon scattering under high power density reduces the effective bulk phonon mean free path and alters the spectral overlap for interface transmission, thereby shifting the critical threshold where interface resistance dominates, distinct from shifts caused by electron-phonon decoupling or defect generation.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Measurement of the crossover point between bulk-dominated and interface-dominated thermal resistance as a function of interface bonding topology and applied power density, using frequency-domain or time-domain thermoreflectance to extract spectrally resolved transmission and effective MFP, while independently monitoring electron temperature and structural integrity to rule out confounders.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Spectrally resolved measurements of interface thermal conductance and bulk thermal conductivity under varying power densities to extract the effective MFP and transmission function, demonstrating the predicted shift in the crossover threshold, alongside independent verification that electron temperatures and structural states remain within the reversible phonon-dominated regime.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Survey anchors indicate the maximum transmission limit is reliable for clean interfaces but unresolved for heterogeneous ones, and that no boundary variable has been systematically varied to demonstrate the crossover. The revision aligns the mechanism with these unresolved heterogeneous conditions while bounding the scope against known high-flux confounders.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The model fails or the mechanism is confounded if the interface transmission is dominated by localized defect states, if high power density induces irreversible structural changes (e.g., electromigration, phase transformation, interfacial sliding), or if electron-phonon non-equilibrium becomes the primary driver of thermal resistance changes (e.g., in highly doped semiconductors or metals at extreme fluxes).
hypothesis.claim_scope: Establish quantitative boundary conditions for the maximum transmission limit model by identifying the critical spectrally resolved interface transmission threshold where interface resistance overtakes bulk resistance, and validate this threshold under high-power-density operating conditions specifically bounded to regimes where reversible lattice phonon-phonon scattering dominates over electron-phonon decoupling and irreversible structural degradation.
assumptions: Interface transmission probability can be parameterized by a spectrally resolved transmission function that accounts for bonding topology and chemical heterogeneity.
High power density induces reversible non-equilibrium phonon-phonon scattering without causing irreversible structural degradation or dominant electron-phonon decoupling at the interface.
The crossover threshold is material-pair specific but follows predictable scaling laws based on the spectrally resolved transmission function within the defined validity domain.

mature_idea.scientific_object: High-power-density materials (wide-bandgap semiconductors, doped thermoelectrics, metallic thin films) under controlled carrier density and temperature gradients
assumptions: Wiedemann-Franz law deviations can be attributed primarily to electron-phonon coupling rather than other scattering mechanisms
Spectral phonon imaging has sufficient resolution to distinguish phonon contributions from electron contributions
Carrier density variations do not significantly alter phonon dispersion or scattering rates
The material system allows independent control of carrier density without introducing additional defect scattering
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
mature_idea.falsifier: Demonstration that phonon and electron contributions cannot be independently varied or measured with sufficient precision to distinguish their relative contributions, or that Wiedemann-Franz deviations are dominated by mechanisms other than electron-phonon coupling
