directions.title: Decoupling Phonon and Electron Heat Conduction via Carrier Density-Temperature Variation and Spectral Phonon Imaging
directions.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials can be discriminated by replacing isotopic mass variance tuning with controlled variations in carrier density via electrostatic gating and temperature, combined with spectrally-resolved phonon transport characterization to directly resolve phonon mean free path distributions. By systematically perturbing carrier density without introducing chemical dopants, we avoid ionized impurity scattering confounders and exploit the differential response of each carrier type—isolating electron thermal conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law baseline with a calibrated Lorenz number while tracking phonon transport. Spectrally-resolved phonon transport characterization provides the discriminating observation to partition carrier contributions, bounded by the failure threshold where extreme power densities induce non-linear electron-phonon coupling or dielectric breakdown. This resolves the identifiability gap by providing a direct mechanistic partition of heat dissipation limits.

trace.opponent_concern: Heavy doping to vary carrier density inevitably introduces ionized impurity scattering, which strongly suppresses phonon thermal conductivity via point-defect scattering. This confounds the decoupling, as both electron and phonon contributions change simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate the pure carrier density effect on electrons without a precise model of the impurity scattering effect on phonons.

mature_idea.scientific_object: Twisted multilayer van der Waals heterostructures (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) with controlled interlayer rotation angles
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

directions.title: Moiré Potential Landscapes Dictate the Thermal Cycling Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: Engineered interlayer twist angles suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures, but their stability under operational thermal cycling remains unverified across diverse materials. We replace the complex shear-strain locking mechanism with a fundamental boundary condition governed by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape. We demonstrate that engineered twist angles remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, and in the absence of confounding defect-mediated or chemically-induced pinning. By synthesizing heterostructures across diverse material families and subjecting them to controlled thermal cycling, we isolate the moiré potential mechanism and establish the material-dependent limits of thermal anisotropy retention.

trace.scientific_concern: The candidate conflates 'random interlayer rotations' with a 'twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.' A moiré potential landscape requires a well-defined, uniform twist angle to form a periodic superlattice. Random rotations would result in a spatially disordered potential that does not provide coherent energy barriers to pin specific twist angles.
trace.opponent_concern: If the interlayer rotations are truly random, the moiré potential is spatially varying and averages out, meaning it cannot act as a coherent pinning mechanism for structural stability. The mechanism only holds if the twist angles are specifically engineered and uniform.
trace.required_revision: Replace 'random interlayer rotations' and 'rotational disorder' with 'engineered twist angles' or 'controlled interlayer twist angles' to maintain consistency with the moiré potential mechanism.
alternative_explanations: Thermal cycling induces interlayer diffusion or chemical bonding that pins the layers independently of the moiré potential.
Changes in thermal contact resistance during cycling mimic changes in intrinsic cross-plane thermal conductivity.

directions.title: Thermal Cycling Limits of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
directions.abstract: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in nanoscale devices is bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet degradation mechanisms under high thermal loads remain unverified. We propose that when thermal energy exceeds the activation barrier for in-plane interlayer slip, it induces thermally activated local twist-angle disorder and interfacial defect formation, replacing static moiré phonon scattering models. We perform thermal cycling degradation tests on suspended or rigidly supported twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2), measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity before and after cycling, and quantifying twist angle distribution changes via electron diffraction. Cross-sectional STEM is used to explicitly rule out interfacial delamination and substrate wrinkling. Molecular dynamics simulations determine the activation energy barriers for in-plane interlayer slip, validated against experiment. This provides direct observation of thermal transport ceilings and structural stability limits across multiple TMD systems.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: When thermal energy exceeds the activation barrier for in-plane interlayer slip in suspended or rigidly supported twisted TMD heterostructures, it induces thermally activated local twist-angle disorder and interfacial defect formation, rather than substrate strain relaxation or delamination, which fundamentally limits cross-plane thermal transport under high power density.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Thermal loads provide sufficient activation energy to overcome the in-plane interlayer shear/sliding energy barrier, causing local twist-angle variations and the formation of interfacial defects that strongly scatter phonons and increase interfacial thermal resistance, without inducing out-of-plane separation.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Direct measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation correlated with quantitative in-plane twist angle distribution broadening via electron diffraction, alongside cross-sectional STEM imaging to explicitly rule out interfacial delamination, blistering, or substrate-induced wrinkling.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Empirical observation of thermal conductivity degradation concurrent with in-plane twist angle distribution broadening via electron diffraction and absence of out-of-plane delamination via cross-sectional STEM, bounded by molecular dynamics predictions of activation energy barriers for in-plane interlayer slip.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Empirical thermal conductivity measurements, electron diffraction patterns, cross-sectional STEM imaging, and molecular dynamics simulations of twisted TMD interfaces.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds for twist angles and TMD combinations where thermal cycling remains below the chemical degradation and delamination thresholds, and where substrate-induced strain is minimized (e.g., via suspended membranes or rigid matched substrates); it fails if out-of-plane separation, blistering, or substrate wrinkling is the primary driver of thermal resistance.

trace.target_claim: Exceeding a critical binding energy threshold in twisted TMD heterostructures induces thermally activated moiré superlattice relaxation and localized defect-mediated phonon scattering, which fundamentally limits cross-plane thermal transport under high power density.
trace.scientific_concern: The phrase 'exceeding a critical binding energy threshold' is physically inaccurate, as thermal loads provide kinetic energy to overcome activation barriers for interlayer slip/rotation, rather than 'exceeding' a static binding energy. Additionally, 'thermal cycling ablation' is a misnomer; 'ablation' refers to material removal, whereas the context implies thermal fatigue or degradation. Finally, conflating 'moiré superlattice relaxation' with 'localized amorphous defects' conflates elastic twist-angle variation with irreversible structural amorphization.
trace.opponent_concern: The proposed mechanism conflates reversible interlayer slip (which alters the local moiré period) with irreversible amorphization, making it unclear whether the observed thermal resistance increase is due to moiré period changes or permanent structural damage.
trace.required_revision: Revise the mechanism to state that thermal energy overcomes the activation barrier for interlayer slip/rotation, inducing local twist-angle disorder rather than 'exceeding binding energy'. Replace 'thermal cycling ablation' with 'thermal cycling degradation'. Clarify whether the structural change is reversible twist-angle variation or irreversible defect formation.
alternative_explanations: The increase in interfacial thermal resistance under thermal cycling is primarily due to the generation of irreversible point defects and vacancies (e.g., chalcogen vacancies) rather than reversible interlayer slip or moiré period changes.
Thermal expansion mismatch between the layers induces reversible elastic strain that temporarily increases phonon scattering without permanent structural relaxation.
trace.final_scope: Twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures (MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2) subjected to high power density thermal cycling, where thermal energy exceeds the activation barrier for interlayer slip.

directions.title: Cyclic Hysteresis and Residual State Mapping of Structural Stability Boundaries in Twist-Angle-Engineered Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) assumes structural stability under operational thermal loads, but the fundamental limits of this stability under high power density remain unclear. We investigate the thermally induced interfacial strain mechanism to identify the critical strain thresholds governing moiré lattice distortion. By applying incremental high-power-density thermal cycling and quantifying residual changes in cross-plane thermal conductivity and moiré diffraction spot splitting via time-domain thermoreflectance and nanobeam electron diffraction, we isolate the onset of irreversible interfacial strain accumulation from reversible phonon-phonon scattering. This approach maps the structural stability boundaries across MoS2/WS2 and other TMDs, establishing precise power-density limits where moiré phonon localization degrades due to permanent strain-induced moiré distortion, while strictly bounding the system below the threshold for interfacial decohesion.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in TMD heterostructures under high power density is bounded by a critical interfacial strain threshold for moiré lattice distortion, which manifests as irreversible residual hysteresis in cross-plane Kapitza resistance and moiré diffraction spot splitting, distinguishing thermally induced interfacial strain accumulation from reversible phonon-phonon scattering.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Apply incremental high-power-density thermal cycling to perturb the twist-angle-engineered TMD heterostructure, and characterize the residual state via cross-plane Kapitza resistance and moiré diffraction spot splitting hysteresis to bound the critical interfacial strain threshold for moiré lattice distortion.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Thermally induced interfacial strain accumulation at the twist-angle boundaries irreversibly distorts the moiré superlattice, degrading moiré phonon localization and causing a permanent increase in Kapitza resistance that persists after thermal relaxation, distinguishing it from reversible phonon-phonon scattering and avoiding catastrophic interfacial decohesion.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparing the residual cross-plane Kapitza resistance and NBED moiré diffraction spot splitting after incremental thermal cycling against open-loop fixed-load thermal cycling to isolate the irreversible hysteresis loop of interfacial strain accumulation from transient thermal saturation and reversible phonon scattering.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of residual cross-plane Kapitza resistance increases and corresponding moiré diffraction spot splitting in twist-angle-engineered TMDs after incremental high-power-density thermal cycling, with rigorous structural decoupling to confirm the absence of phase transitions or point defects, validated against molecular dynamics predictions of interfacial strain.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of residual cross-plane Kapitza resistance and moiré diffraction spot splitting in twist-angle-engineered TMDs after incremental high-power-density thermal cycling, contrasted with open-loop controls and validated via molecular dynamics, contingent on successful decoupling from alternative defect mechanisms.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim fails if thermal cycling induces irreversible 2H-to-1T phase transitions, chalcogen vacancy generation, or substrate delamination rather than pure interfacial strain accumulation. Rigorous structural decoupling via NBED and Raman spectroscopy is required to rule out these alternative defect mechanisms, and the power density must be strictly bounded below the decohesion threshold.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Limits of Heat Transfer in Matter, specifically the structural stability boundaries and thermally induced interfacial strain mechanisms in twist-angle-engineered TMD heterostructures under high power density, bounded by the critical strain threshold for moiré lattice distortion and strictly excluding catastrophic decohesion or phase transitions.
assumptions: Assumes that residual changes in cross-plane Kapitza resistance and moiré diffraction spot splitting can be rigorously decoupled from irreversible phase transitions and point defect generation using combined NBED and Raman characterization.
Assumes that the thermal cycling bounds are tightly constrained below the threshold for interfacial decohesion and bulk lattice degradation, isolating the interfacial strain regime.

directions.title: Stability Limits of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: Fundamental heat transfer limits in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the stability of twist-angle-engineered interfaces under high power density remains unverified. We establish a closed-loop metrology framework linking direct thermal characterization to high-power thermal cycling, revealing the thermal loading thresholds where thermally activated interlayer sliding and stacking disorder degrade moiré phonon transport. By quantifying local registry shifts via low-dose nanobeam electron diffraction and extending validation across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides, we define the structural stability boundary conditions for moiré thermal transport. This provides the missing direct observation of interfacial thermal limits, resolving target object and evidence deficits while explicitly decoupling electron beam damage and transducer thermal boundary resistance confounders.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The cross-plane thermal conductivity of twist-angle-engineered TMD interfaces degrades under high power density due to thermally activated interlayer sliding and local stacking disorder, which alters the moiré phonon scattering landscape, rather than intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering limits, provided that electron beam-induced defect generation and transducer/substrate thermal boundary resistance variations are strictly controlled and decoupled.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: High power density thermal loading induces local thermal stresses and provides activation energy that overcomes the moiré potential corrugation, causing thermally activated interlayer sliding and stacking disorder that alters the moiré phonon scattering landscape and increases interfacial thermal resistance, independent of electron beam-induced point defects.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Direct observation of cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation correlating with quantified local stacking disorder via low-dose nanobeam electron diffraction, distinguishing interfacial structural sliding from intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering saturation, electron beam-induced defect scattering, and transducer/substrate thermal boundary resistance changes.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity via TDTR before and after thermal cycling, correlated with local stacking disorder maps from low-dose nanobeam electron diffraction, and validated against molecular dynamics predictions of moiré potential corrugation, while explicitly demonstrating that thermal resistance changes are not attributable to electron beam damage or transducer/substrate TBR variations.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements of cross-plane thermal conductivity with differential interface modeling, low-dose nanobeam electron diffraction for local stacking disorder, and molecular dynamics simulations of moiré potential corrugation.

directions.title: Closed-Loop Metrology-Driven Tuning of Atomic Interfacial Bonding to Isolate Phonon Transmission Limits in Metal-Dielectric Heterostructures
directions.abstract: High-power-density heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics is fundamentally bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the atomic-scale bonding mechanisms governing this limit remain obscured. We introduce a highly feasible, systematic structural tuning approach where controlled thermal annealing incrementally alters the atomic interfacial bonding state of metal-dielectric heterostructures, guided by precision thermal metrology. By strictly constraining the annealing window to prevent bulk property evolution and morphological changes, and correlating step-wise structural perturbations with in-situ thermal transport characterization, we isolate the specific phonon transmission mechanisms that dictate thermal saturation. This stable, mechanism-specific framework reliably evaluates thermal dissipation boundaries under extreme power densities by decoupling interfacial bonding effects from bulk and morphological confounders.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Systematic, step-wise controlled annealing, constrained to prevent bulk property evolution and morphological changes, allows the atomic interfacial bonding state to be deterministically tuned and characterized via precision thermal metrology, isolating the phonon transmission mechanism that saturates interfacial thermal resistance.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Incremental thermal annealing systematically alters the atomic interfacial bonding state without altering bulk thermal properties or interfacial morphology, while precision thermal metrology characterizes the resulting thermal transport, allowing the specific phonon transmission mechanism that bounds the interfacial thermal resistance to be isolated.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Observation of a distinct saturation threshold in interfacial thermal resistance that correlates directly with a specific, metrologically verified atomic interfacial bonding state, while bulk thermal conductivity and interfacial morphology remain invariant, which disappears upon interfacial bonding ablation.

directions.title: Isolating Bond-Stiffness-Limited Phonon Transmission at Epitaxial Metal-Dielectric Interfaces via Coherent Strain-Mediated Bond Stiffness Modulation
directions.abstract: The fundamental phenomenon of bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission at epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces remains obscured by defect scattering, bulk phonon density of states (DOS) modifications, and electronic coupling artifacts. We replace dynamic defect-tuned phonon scattering with coherent strain-mediated bond stiffness modulation as the primary causal mechanism for isolating the minimum interfacial thermal resistance. By synthesizing a lattice-mismatch strain series of ultra-thin epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces (e.g., Ag/MgO < 5 nm) while preserving coherency through low-temperature annealing, we directly modulate interfacial bond compression without introducing defect scattering. Precision time-domain thermoreflectance metrology maps Kapitza resistance against density-functional-theory-calculated bond stiffness, while explicitly bounding bulk phonon DOS changes and subtracting electron-phonon coupling variations. Ablation against a deliberately defected comparator series isolates the bond-stiffness mechanism from defect-mediated scattering, establishing the phenomenon and its high-power-density failure boundary.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Coherent strain-mediated bond stiffness modulation directly dictates the minimum interfacial thermal resistance by isolating bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission in ultra-thin epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces, provided that strain-induced bulk phonon DOS modifications and interfacial electronic variations are strictly bounded and decoupled.

scientific_object.description: ultra_thin_epitaxial_metal_dielectric_interface

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Coherent strain-mediated bond stiffness modulation directly dictates the minimum interfacial thermal resistance by isolating bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission, independent of defect-mediated phonon scattering, provided strain-induced bulk phonon DOS changes and electronic variations are decoupled.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Synthesizing a lattice-mismatch strain series of ultra-thin epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces (e.g., Ag/MgO < 5 nm) using low-temperature annealing to modulate interfacial bond compression while preserving coherency, contrasted against a deliberately defected comparator series, while simultaneously characterizing and bounding bulk phonon DOS shifts.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Varying the lattice mismatch systematically alters the interfacial bond stiffness, which directly modulates the phonon transmission spectra across the interface, thereby bounding the minimum interfacial thermal resistance without the confounding effects of defect scattering, bulk phonon DOS alterations, or significant electronic band structure changes.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Correlating precision time-domain thermoreflectance measurements of Kapitza resistance with density-functional-theory-calculated bond stiffness across the coherent strain series, while explicitly modeling and subtracting the contributions of strain-induced bulk phonon DOS shifts and electron-phonon coupling variations, and demonstrating a deviation from this correlation in the defect scattering ablation series.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Measurement of Kapitza resistance via precision thermal metrology across the coherent strain series and the defect scattering ablation series, correlated with DFT-calculated bond stiffness, while explicitly bounding bulk phonon DOS shifts and electron-phonon coupling, to demonstrate the isolation of the bond-stiffness limit.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Precision time-domain thermoreflectance measurements of Kapitza resistance correlated with DFT-calculated bond stiffness and bounded bulk phonon DOS shifts across a coherent strain series in ultra-thin systems, contrasted against a deliberately defected comparator series.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission mechanism fails or saturates when the film thickness exceeds the critical thickness for coherent strain (inducing misfit dislocations), when high power density triggers phonon-phonon scattering and strain relaxation, when bulk phonon DOS modifications dominate the thermal transport changes, or when strain-induced electronic effects dominate the thermal boundary resistance.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Limits of Heat Transfer in Matter, specifically the isolation of bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission at ultra-thin epitaxial metal-dielectric interfaces under coherent strain, strictly decoupled from bulk phonon DOS modifications and interfacial electronic effects.
assumptions: The selected ultra-thin metal-dielectric pairs (e.g., Ag/MgO < 5 nm) can sustain coherent strain without forming misfit dislocations.
Strain-induced changes in the bulk phonon density of states can be accurately calculated via DFT and bounded experimentally to isolate the interfacial bond-stiffness effect.
Electron-phonon coupling variations due to strain can be accurately modeled and decoupled from the phonon transmission limit using two-temperature models.

directions.falsifier: A result showing that Kapitza resistance variations across the coherent strain series are entirely dominated by strain-induced bulk phonon DOS changes or electron-phonon coupling variations, rather than by the interfacial bond-stiffness limit.
directions.gap_alignment: Resolves the unmapped_gap:phenomenon by replacing defect-mediated dynamic tuning with coherent strain-mediated bond stiffness modulation in physically feasible ultra-thin systems, providing a direct causal pathway to isolate bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission while explicitly bounding competing bulk and electronic mechanisms.

trace.target_claim: Coherent strain-mediated bond stiffness modulation directly dictates the minimum interfacial thermal resistance by isolating bond-stiffness-limited phonon transmission, independent of defect-mediated phonon scattering.
trace.scientific_concern: The proposed material systems (Au/MgO and Cu/Si) have lattice mismatches (~13% and ~10% respectively) far exceeding the critical thickness for coherent strain, making the coherent strain series physically unfeasible and highly likely to fail due to immediate misfit dislocation formation. Additionally, strain alters electronic band structures, meaning changes in Kapitza resistance could be driven by modified electron-phonon coupling rather than purely phonon bond-stiffness.
trace.opponent_concern: Strain-induced modifications to the electronic density of states and electron-phonon coupling at the interface may independently dictate thermal boundary resistance, confounding the isolation of the pure phonon bond-stiffness limit.
trace.required_revision: Revise the material system to ultra-thin epitaxial metal-dielectric pairs (e.g., Ag/MgO < 5 nm) to ensure physical feasibility of coherent strain. Refine the mechanism to explicitly account for and decouple strain-induced changes in electron-phonon coupling from pure phonon bond-stiffness effects.

directions.title: Iterative Interfacial Bonding Tuning to Isolate the Optical Phonon Bottleneck Limit in Graphene-Substrate Interfaces
directions.abstract: The fundamental limit of heat dissipation in graphene-substrate interfaces under high power density is governed by a non-equilibrium optical phonon bottleneck. Identifying the structural state that maximizes thermal boundary conductance requires precise mapping of interfacial bonding without introducing confounding intrinsic defect scattering. We implement a systematic structural perturbation of the graphene-substrate interface via controlled, strictly interfacial stable covalent functionalization density. By precisely mapping the phonon spectral overlap and anharmonic coupling pathways as a function of this stable interfacial state, we isolate the optimal atomic-scale bonding configuration that suppresses the bottleneck. Comparison against static, unoptimized baselines and stress testing under extreme heat flux confirms that the identified saturation limit is a fundamental phonon property rather than an artifact of thermal degradation, dynamic instability, or intrinsic basal plane scattering.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The fundamental limit of thermal boundary conductance under high power density in graphene-substrate interfaces is governed by a non-equilibrium optical phonon bottleneck, which can be maximized by systematically tuning a strictly interfacial stable covalent bonding density to optimize phonon spectral overlap and anharmonic coupling pathways, provided intrinsic in-plane defect scattering is decoupled.

hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparison of the thermal boundary conductance saturation threshold between the systematically perturbed strictly interfacial stable interface and a static, unoptimized baseline, demonstrating a distinct saturation ceiling that vanishes at low power densities, while confirming via Raman mapping that the intrinsic in-plane thermal conductivity of the graphene remains unperturbed.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of the thermal boundary conductance saturation threshold via precision thermal metrology under high power density, contrasting the systematically perturbed strictly interfacial stable interface with a static baseline, coupled with structural characterization confirming the absence of basal plane defect scattering.

directions.title: Spectroscopy-Driven Interfacial Boundary Calibration for Kinetic Phonon Transport Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet kinetic transport models lack a calibrated boundary variable to accurately predict the transition from bulk-limited to interface-limited regimes. We replace static interfacial boundary assumptions with a phonon spectroscopy-constrained boundary calibration mechanism. Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy extracts phonon mean free paths and transmission coefficients at heterointerfaces, which are used to a priori parameterize the interfacial boundary condition within a kinetic phonon transport model. This mechanism replacement shifts the paradigm from static acoustic mismatch assumptions to spectroscopy-constrained boundary calibration, resolving the unmapped boundary variable gap and bounding the thermal transport limit under high power density.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Calibrating the interfacial boundary condition a priori using mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy data (phonon mean free path and transmission coefficients) from representative heterostructures produces quantitatively accurate predictions of thermal transport limits under high power density, whereas static boundary assumptions (acoustic mismatch model) systematically mispredict the transition from bulk-limited to interface-limited heat dissipation regimes.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy captures the actual phonon transmission and scattering physics at the interface, including mode-specific contributions to Kapitza resistance. By using this characterization data to parameterize the kinetic transport model's boundary condition a priori, the model reflects real material-specific interface behavior rather than idealized acoustic impedance matching, enabling accurate prediction of when and how interface resistance dominates over bulk conduction.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparison of predicted Kapitza resistance and thermal transport limit between the spectroscopy-calibrated kinetic model and the static AMM/DMM model against direct experimental measurements across the transition from bulk-limited to interface-limited regimes; the calibrated model should match measured thermal transport limits within experimental uncertainty where the static model fails.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy measurements demonstrating that the a priori calibrated interfacial boundary condition predicts Kapitza resistance and thermal transport limit more accurately than static AMM/DMM assumptions, specifically in the interface-limited regime. Evidence must also identify the power density threshold where the calibration breaks down due to non-equilibrium optical phonon effects.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Phonon spectroscopy data providing mode-resolved mean free paths, and thermal transport limit measurements under high power density.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The calibration mechanism fails when non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations dominate interfacial transport under extreme power density, causing the acoustic-phonon-based boundary calibration to become invalid. The failure threshold occurs when optical phonon generation rates exceed interfacial transit rates, decoupling the calibrated boundary condition from actual heat dissipation behavior.

Representative heterostructures used for spectroscopy accurately reflect the interface physics of the operational nanoscale devices.

mature_idea.title: Dynamic Twist Angle Tuning via Strain-Mediated Moiré Potential Modulation
mature_idea.abstract: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_idea.hypothesis: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_idea.central_hypothesis: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_idea.mechanism: Apply controlled biaxial strain to twisted van der Waals heterostructures while measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity. Use piezoelectric actuators or thermal expansion mismatch to modulate strain dynamically. Correlate strain-induced moiré potential changes with thermal conductivity variations. This tests whether twist-angle engineering can be made adaptive rather than static.
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Apply controlled biaxial strain to twisted van der Waals heterostructures while measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity. Use piezoelectric actuators or thermal expansion mismatch to modulate strain dynamically. Correlate strain-induced moiré potential changes with thermal conductivity variations. This tests whether twist-angle engineering can be made adaptive rather than static.
mature_idea.falsifier: Measure cross-plane thermal conductivity as a function of applied strain (0-2% biaxial) in twisted MoS2 heterostructures. Use ultrafast X-ray diffraction to track moiré pattern changes under strain. Compare experimental results to molecular dynamics predictions of strain-dependent moiré potentials. Validate that thermal conductivity can be tuned by >20% via strain modulation.

directions.title: Strain-Mediated Moiré Potential Modulation for Adaptive Cross-Plane Thermal Conductivity in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
directions.abstract: Instead of assuming direct strain-tuned phonon transport, we establish the moiré potential landscape as the definitive structural mediator, resolving measurement construct mismatches in twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy. By applying controlled biaxial mechanical strain to twisted MoS2/WS2 heterostructures, we dynamically alter the moiré potential landscape and measure the resulting cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time. In-situ nanobeam electron diffraction characterizes the in-plane moiré periodicity, while cross-plane structural characterization bounds the Poisson-induced interlayer spacing changes. This representation shift from direct strain-phonon coupling to strain-moiré-phonon coupling provides a falsifiable, invariant-based mechanism for adaptive thermal management, explicitly isolated from direct van der Waals gap variations.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain actively tunes cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides, with the moiré-mediated interfacial effect isolated from direct strain-phonon coupling, intrinsic layer conductivity changes, and direct Poisson-induced interlayer spacing variations via untwisted bilayer controls and out-of-plane structural tracking.

scientific_object.description: twisted MoS2/WS2 van der Waals heterostructures under dynamic biaxial strain

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Strain-mediated moiré potential modulation, where applied mechanical strain alters the moiré superlattice periodicity and potential depth to modulate interfacial phonon scattering rates, decoupled from direct changes in interlayer van der Waals spacing.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Applying controlled biaxial mechanical strain (0-2%) via piezoelectric actuators to perturb the moiré potential landscape of twisted MoS2/WS2 heterostructures while simultaneously tracking out-of-plane interlayer spacing.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Strain alters the moiré superlattice periodicity and potential depth, which modulates interfacial phonon scattering rates and cross-plane thermal transport pathways. This effect is explicitly decoupled from the weak direct strain-phonon coupling and the Poisson-ratio-induced reduction in interlayer spacing.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Correlating in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction measurements of moiré periodicity changes with time-domain thermoreflectance measurements of cross-plane thermal conductivity, while simultaneously using cross-plane structural characterization (e.g., cross-plane STEM or XRD) to bound interlayer spacing changes, and comparing against untwisted bilayer controls.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity as a function of applied strain, correlated with in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction tracking of moiré periodicity changes and cross-plane structural tracking of interlayer spacing, validated against molecular dynamics predictions, with untwisted controls used to decouple intrinsic layer effects.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Experimental measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity via TDTR correlated with in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction of moiré periodicity and out-of-plane structural characterization, validated against molecular dynamics simulations of strain-dependent moiré potentials and interlayer spacing.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails if interlayer slip or moiré superlattice relaxation occurs under dynamic strain, if thermal contact resistance variations dominate the TDTR signal, or if the observed thermal conductivity tuning scales linearly with the Poisson-induced reduction in interlayer spacing rather than the moiré periodicity. The structural stability boundary is defined by the critical binding energy threshold and a 2% strain limit.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Twisted transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures under dynamic biaxial strain up to 2%, where moiré-mediated interfacial thermal resistance is isolated from intrinsic layer strain-phonon effects and direct Poisson-induced interlayer spacing variations.
assumptions: The moiré superlattice remains structurally stable without interlayer slip under the applied strain limits.
Thermal contact resistance variations are negligible compared to intrinsic moiré-mediated phonon scattering.

Poisson-induced out-of-plane strain and interlayer spacing changes are either negligible within the 2% biaxial strain limit or can be explicitly measured and decoupled from the moiré periodicity effects.

directions.falsifier: Measure cross-plane thermal conductivity as a function of applied strain (0-2% biaxial) in twisted MoS2 heterostructures. Use in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction to track moiré pattern changes and cross-plane methods to track interlayer spacing. If the thermal conductivity tuning correlates primarily with the reduction in interlayer spacing rather than the moiré periodicity, or if untwisted controls show equivalent tuning, the moiré-mediated mechanism is falsified.
directions.gap_alignment: Addresses the limits of heat transfer in matter by identifying material-dependent limits on interfacial thermal resistance and phonon heat conduction under high power density via adaptive moiré potential modulation, strictly bounded against direct structural confounders.

trace.target_claim: Dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain actively tunes cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides, independent of direct strain-phonon coupling or intrinsic layer conductivity changes.
trace.scientific_concern: The use of 'ultrafast X-ray diffraction' to resolve nanometer-scale moiré superlattice periodicity changes is physically inconsistent, as ultrafast XRD primarily probes atomic-scale lattice dynamics rather than nanometer-scale superlattice envelopes. Furthermore, claiming the thermal response is strictly 'independent' of direct strain-phonon coupling and intrinsic layer conductivity changes is overly strong, as biaxial strain inherently alters the phonon dispersion of the constituent TMD layers.
trace.opponent_concern: Ultrafast XRD cannot resolve the moiré superlattice periodicity in 2D materials; strain will inevitably change the intrinsic phonon dispersion of the MoS2/WS2 layers, confounding the isolation of the moiré-mediated interfacial effect.
trace.required_revision: Replace 'ultrafast X-ray diffraction' with 'in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction' for moiré periodicity tracking. Revise the hypothesis to state that the moiré-mediated effect is 'isolated from' direct strain-phonon coupling via untwisted controls, rather than claiming absolute independence.
alternative_explanations: Changes in cross-plane thermal conductivity are primarily driven by strain-induced modifications to the intrinsic phonon dispersion and Grüneisen parameters of the individual TMD layers, rather than moiré potential modulation.
Variations in thermal contact resistance or interlayer spacing (Poisson effect) dominate the TDTR signal, masking any moiré-mediated phonon scattering effects.
trace.final_scope: Twisted transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures under dynamic biaxial strain up to 2%, where moiré-mediated interfacial thermal resistance is isolated from intrinsic layer strain-phonon effects.

trace.scientific_concern: Direct strain-induced changes in interlayer van der Waals gap distance (via the Poisson effect) or intrinsic layer phonon dispersion could confound the observed changes in cross-plane thermal conductivity, making it unclear if the moiré potential modulation is the true mediator.

alternative_explanations: Direct Poisson-ratio-induced reduction in interlayer van der Waals spacing enhancing cross-plane phonon transmission.

directions.title: Kinetic Time-Temperature-Transformation Mapping of Interfacial Rotational Slip in Twisted van der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered van der Waals heterostructures offer tunable thermal transport, but operational stability under high power density is limited by interfacial relaxation. We replace the assumption of a static thermodynamic stability threshold with a kinetic time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram to resolve measurement construct mismatches in predicting structural relaxation. By closing the loop between in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction and adaptive thermal cycling, we map critical temperature-time combinations where twist angles remain stable versus relax. We validate this kinetic framework by correlating twist-angle distribution changes with cross-plane thermal conductivity, determining critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics, and extending the stability phase diagram across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides. Crucially, we isolate pure rotational slip from confounding in-plane translational sliding, defect-mediated relaxation, and thermal expansion-induced delamination. This representation shift exposes the activation barrier invariant for interfacial slip, providing a predictive boundary for twist-angle engineering.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The structural relaxation of twist-angle-engineered van der Waals heterostructures under thermal stress is governed by a kinetic activation barrier for pure interfacial rotational slip, which can be mapped as a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram, provided that in-plane translational sliding, defect-mediated relaxation, and thermal expansion-induced delamination are explicitly ruled out as the primary drivers of thermal transport degradation.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Interfacial rotational slip requires overcoming a specific activation energy barrier that depends on both temperature and time; mapping this kinetic boundary exposes the invariant slip barrier and allows predictive determination of structural stability under varying thermal loads, strictly discriminated from in-plane Moire translation and defect accumulation.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Time-dependent twist-angle relaxation at constant sub-critical temperatures, with a corresponding shift in cross-plane thermal conductivity, while explicitly ruling out in-plane Moire pattern translation, defect accumulation, and interfacial delamination via distinct nanobeam diffraction symmetry and thickness-profile signatures.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Observation of time-dependent twist-angle relaxation at constant sub-critical temperatures, accompanied by a corresponding shift in cross-plane thermal conductivity, with concurrent diffraction evidence ruling out in-plane translation, defect accumulation, and delamination.

hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The kinetic TTT representation fails if twist-angle relaxation is purely thermodynamic, if alternative mechanisms like in-plane layer sliding or defect-mediated relaxation dominate over interfacial rotational slip, or if thermal expansion-induced delamination alters the thermal endpoint without actual interfacial slip.

Pure rotational slip produces a distinct nanobeam electron diffraction symmetry signature that can be unambiguously separated from in-plane translational sliding and defect-induced peak broadening.

mature_idea.scientific_object: Heterogeneous material interfaces (metal-semiconductor, dielectric-substrate, van der Waals junctions) with systematically varied bonding strength and contamination levels
assumptions: Interface transmission probability can be parameterized by a single effective bonding energy metric
Bulk phonon mean free path distribution remains invariant under moderate power density increases
Non-equilibrium optical phonon populations do not significantly alter interface transmission coefficients
The crossover threshold is material-pair specific but follows predictable scaling laws
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

mature_idea.falsifier: Demonstration that no universal bonding energy threshold exists across different material systems, or that the threshold shifts unpredictably under high power density due to non-equilibrium effects not captured by the proposed scaling law

route_signature.scientific_object: Heterogeneous material interfaces (metal-semiconductor, dielectric-substrate, van der Waals junctions) with systematically varied bonding strength and contamination levels
assumptions: Interface transmission probability can be parameterized by a single effective bonding energy metric
Bulk phonon mean free path distribution remains invariant under moderate power density increases
Non-equilibrium optical phonon populations do not significantly alter interface transmission coefficients
The crossover threshold is material-pair specific but follows predictable scaling laws
route_signature.mechanism_or_relation: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

directions.title: Flux-Dependent Spectral Transmission Threshold for the Bulk-to-Interface Thermal Resistance Crossover
directions.abstract: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance is traditionally modeled using static acoustic mismatch or equilibrium bonding energy thresholds. We propose a representation shift: defining the critical crossover boundary through the flux-dependent spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations. By modulating interface bonding energy and applying high-power-density heat flux, we demonstrate that the critical threshold shifts predictably as hot phonons alter the effective transmission probability via anharmonic interactions. This non-equilibrium spectral transmission model resolves the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit for weakly bonded interfaces and identifies the precise boundary variable governing the crossover under operational conditions, explicitly decoupled from local thermal expansion and equilibrium bulk scattering artifacts.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The critical interface bonding energy threshold for the bulk-to-interface thermal resistance crossover shifts predictably as a function of the spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations, mediated by anharmonic interactions, under high heat flux, independent of local thermal expansion or equilibrium temperature-dependent bulk scattering.
hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Flux-dependent spectral transmission threshold mediated by anharmonic phonon interactions, decoupled from equilibrium thermal expansion and bulk scattering
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Rewire the experimental characterization loop such that ultrafast spectral phonon characterization directly informs iterative interface bonding energy modulation to pinpoint the flux-dependent crossover boundary, followed by isotopic mean free path ablation, mechanical constraint of the interface, and high power density heat flux stress.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: High-power-density heat flux generates a non-equilibrium population of hot phonons, which alters the effective transmission probability and spectral overlap at the interface via anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions, thereby shifting the critical bonding energy threshold where interface resistance overtakes bulk resistance, distinct from shifts caused by local thermal expansion or equilibrium Umklapp scattering.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Observation of a predictable shift in the critical interface bonding energy threshold under varying heat flux densities that persists when local thermal expansion is mechanically constrained and when bulk phonon mean free path is decoupled via isotopic mean free path ablation.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Quantitative mapping of the critical interface bonding energy threshold as a function of heat flux density, corroborated by spectral phonon characterization, isotopic ablation to isolate non-equilibrium phonon effects, and mechanical constraint of the interface to rule out thermal expansion artifacts.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Ultrafast spectral phonon characterization of mechanically constrained Si/Ge heterostructures under varying heat flux densities and isotopic compositions.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The model fails when high power density heat flux stress induces irreversible interface reconstruction, defect generation, bulk thermal runaway, or when local thermal expansion dominates the interface contact mechanics.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Valid for phononic interface systems with weakly to moderately bonded interfaces under quasi-steady-state high heat flux, strictly bounded to regimes where local thermal expansion, stress-induced interface reconstruction, and equilibrium bulk Umklapp scattering are decoupled or accounted for, and before irreversible structural reconstruction or bulk thermal runaway occurs.
assumptions: Non-equilibrium hot phonon populations can be maintained quasi-steady-state via high-repetition-rate ultrafast pumping without causing immediate thermal damage or intermixing.
Anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions are the primary driver of the altered spectral overlap under these non-equilibrium conditions.
Local thermal expansion and stress-induced contact area changes are mechanically constrained or quantitatively decoupled from the spectral transmission measurements.

directions.falsifier: Demonstration that the threshold shift vanishes when non-equilibrium phonons are present but thermal expansion is unconstrained, or that the shift is entirely explained by bulk temperature-dependent thermal conductivity changes and equilibrium Umklapp scattering without requiring a non-equilibrium spectral overlap model.

mature_idea.scientific_object: High-power-density materials (wide-bandgap semiconductors, doped thermoelectrics, metallic thin films) under controlled carrier density and temperature gradients
assumptions: Wiedemann-Franz law deviations can be attributed primarily to electron-phonon coupling rather than other scattering mechanisms
Spectral phonon imaging has sufficient resolution to distinguish phonon contributions from electron contributions
Carrier density variations do not significantly alter phonon dispersion or scattering rates
The material system allows independent control of carrier density without introducing additional defect scattering
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
mature_idea.falsifier: Demonstration that phonon and electron contributions cannot be independently varied or measured with sufficient precision to distinguish their relative contributions, or that Wiedemann-Franz deviations are dominated by mechanisms other than electron-phonon coupling

directions.title: Closed-Loop Spectral Phonon Imaging Reveals Momentum-Resolved Electron-Phonon Bottlenecks in High-Power-Density Heat Dissipation
directions.abstract: The maximum heat dissipation capacity of high-power-density materials is limited by momentum-resolved electron-phonon energy exchange bottlenecks invisible to bulk effective-medium characterization. We introduce an iterative quasi-static representation shift: spectral phonon imaging feedback systematically steers carrier density and temperature perturbations across measurement cycles, converging on momentum-space channels where electron-phonon energy exchange stalls, provided intrinsic scattering dominates over extrinsic limits. This protocol partitions phonon and electron thermal conductivity contributions by exploiting their differential perturbation response—phonons are temperature-sensitive but carrier-density-insensitive, while electrons follow the Wiedemann-Franz law. The invariant exposed is energy flux conservation within converged momentum-space channels; divergence signals the validity boundary where strong correlations or dominant extrinsic scattering break the differential response. We validate through open-loop ablation and extreme-condition stress testing, resolving the identifiability gap in phonon-electron partitioning and establishing bounded validity for high-power-density thermal transport models.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The momentum-resolved electron-phonon energy exchange bottleneck can be directly identified through an iterative quasi-static protocol that systematically perturbs carrier density and temperature and characterizes the resulting momentum-resolved phonon distributions, converging on state-space channels where energy flux conservation partitions phonon and electron contributions to maximum heat dissipation, provided that intrinsic scattering rates exceed extrinsic boundary and defect scattering rates.

scientific_object.description: high-power-density materials (doped wide-bandgap semiconductors and metallic thin films) under iterative carrier density and temperature perturbation in momentum-resolved non-equilibrium state space, bounded by intrinsic scattering dominance

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Momentum-resolved electron-phonon energy exchange bottleneck exposed as a convergent invariant in the iterative quasi-static perturbation state space, where energy flux conservation within specific momentum-space channels distinguishes the mechanism from bulk effective-medium scattering models, contingent on the dominance of intrinsic over extrinsic scattering.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Implement an iterative quasi-static perturbation-characterization protocol that systematically alters carrier density and temperature conditions and characterizes the momentum-resolved phonon distribution, replacing open-loop static characterization with a bounded feedback loop that converges on momentum-space channels where electron-phonon energy exchange stalls, while explicitly bounding extrinsic scattering confounders.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Phonons and electrons respond differentially to perturbation: phonon thermal conductivity is temperature-sensitive but carrier-density-insensitive (governed by intrinsic Umklapp and electron-phonon scattering), while electron thermal conductivity is carrier-density-sensitive via the Wiedemann-Franz law. The iterative protocol exploits this orthogonality by systematically adjusting perturbation conditions between measurement cycles until spectral phonon imaging shows a stable mean-free-path distribution, indicating that the phonon contribution has been isolated from electron-phonon coupling. The remaining thermal conductivity, derived from Wiedemann-Franz deviations, is attributed to electrons. The momentum-resolved bottleneck emerges as the invariant: energy flux conservation within the converged momentum-space channels, assuming extrinsic boundary and defect scattering are sub-dominant.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Convergence of the iterative perturbation-characterization protocol to a stable phonon mean-free-path distribution while carrier density is systematically varied across measurement cycles, demonstrating that phonon and electron thermal conductivity contributions have been partitioned and sum to the measured maximum heat dissipation capacity; divergence or oscillation of the loop indicates the mechanism boundary where the differential response invariant breaks down due to strong correlations or dominant extrinsic scattering.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Observation of stable convergence in spectral phonon mean-free-path distributions under iterative carrier density-temperature perturbation across measurement cycles, demonstrating partitioned phonon and electron thermal conductivity contributions that sum to the measured maximum heat dissipation capacity, while confirming that extrinsic scattering limits do not mask the intrinsic bottleneck.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of iterative quasi-static convergence in spectral phonon imaging, compared against open-loop ablation results, and bounded by stress test failure conditions and extrinsic scattering limits.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds when the Wiedemann-Franz law is approximately satisfied at baseline, spectral phonon imaging energy-momentum resolution exceeds the relevant phonon branch spacing, and intrinsic scattering rates (electron-phonon, phonon-phonon) dominate over extrinsic boundary and defect scattering. It fails when strong electron-electron correlations, non-linear electron-phonon coupling, or dominant extrinsic scattering entangle thermal signatures, causing the iterative protocol to converge on false orthogonality or diverge entirely.

mature_idea.scientific_object: Twisted multilayer van der Waals heterostructures (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) with controlled interlayer rotation angles
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

mature_idea.falsifier: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking within device-relevant thermal cycling conditions (e.g., 1000 cycles between 300 K and 500 K), resulting in recovery of cross-plane conductivity to within 20% of pristine aligned values

directions.title: Thermodynamic Threshold for Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures Under Sustained Thermal Cycling
directions.abstract: Engineered interlayer twist angles designed to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures can degrade under sustained thermal cycling as rotational configurations relax toward equilibrium stacking. We demonstrate that this structural relaxation is governed by a thermodynamic threshold: the engineered anisotropy persists if and only if the interlayer potential corrugation (rotational energy barrier) exceeds a critical barrier defined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, provided that competing mechanisms such as defect evolution and interlayer diffusion are negligible. This representation shift from active feedback stabilization to passive moiré-pinning thresholds exposes the invariant that cross-plane conductivity monotonically tracks interlayer misorientation only when bounded by this energy ratio and isolated from chemical or thermomechanical confounders. The mechanism generalizes from MoS2/WS2 to diverse van der Waals systems (WSe2, MoSe2, graphene/hBN), establishing a material-specific stability boundary for high-power-density thermal management.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Engineered interlayer twist angles in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling if and only if the interlayer potential corrugation exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, provided that competing mechanisms such as point defect evolution and interlayer diffusion are negligible.

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Competition between thermal activation energy and the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential corrugation governing the structural pinning of interlayer twist angles, isolated from defect-mediated and diffusion-mediated thermal transport changes.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Comparing the structural relaxation and cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation of twisted van der Waals heterostructures against their calculated moiré potential corrugation barriers during sustained thermal cycling, while actively monitoring and bounding defect and diffusion confounders.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Interlayer twist angles disrupt coherent phonon tunneling, suppressing cross-plane conductance. The stability of these configurations is governed by the competition between thermal activation energy and the moiré potential corrugation; when the rotational energy barrier exceeds the thermal activation energy, the engineered anisotropy is passively pinned, assuming no concurrent defect generation or interlayer diffusion.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Correlated measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity via TDTR, interlayer twist angle via Raman spectroscopy, and atomic-scale structural/chemical integrity via cross-sectional TEM and EELS, demonstrating that conductivity recovery strictly correlates with rotational relaxation while ruling out defect annealing, interlayer diffusion, or delamination.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking under thermal cycling conditions only when the thermal activation energy exceeds the moiré rotational barrier, resulting in cross-plane conductivity recovery, with concurrent structural and chemical characterization confirming the absence of defect evolution or interlayer diffusion.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Correlated TDTR thermal conductivity measurements, Raman spectroscopy for interlayer twist angle, and cross-sectional TEM/EELS for structural and chemical validation to rule out defect and diffusion confounders under thermal cycling.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim fails when non-thermal relaxation mechanisms (e.g., shear stress, defect-mediated slip, point defect generation/annealing, or interlayer atomic diffusion) dominate the thermal transport changes, or when the interlayer potential corrugation is insufficient to overcome the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Van der Waals heterostructures including MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2, and graphene/hBN with engineered interlayer twist angles under sustained thermal cycling between 300 K and 500 K, strictly in regimes where point defect evolution, interlayer diffusion, and thermomechanical delamination are negligible.
assumptions: Cross-plane thermal conductivity monotonically tracks interlayer twist angle.

Non-thermal relaxation mechanisms, including point defect generation/annealing, interlayer atomic diffusion, and thermomechanical delamination, are negligible under the specified pure thermal cycling conditions.

directions.falsifier: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking within device-relevant thermal cycling conditions, resulting in recovery of cross-plane conductivity, despite the calculated moiré rotational barrier exceeding the thermal activation energy, OR demonstration that conductivity recovery occurs without twist angle relaxation due to defect annealing or interlayer diffusion.
directions.gap_alignment: Resolves the material generality boundary condition by establishing a universal thermodynamic threshold across diverse vdW materials, and resolves the missing assumption of structural stability by defining the moiré rotational energy barrier, while explicitly bounding against structural and chemical confounders.

trace.target_claim: Engineered random interlayer rotations in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling if and only if the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.
trace.scientific_concern: The candidate conflates 'interlayer binding energy' (adhesion energy) with the 'rotational energy barrier' (potential corrugation). Thermal relaxation of twist angles is governed by the energy barrier to rotation (the corrugation of the moiré potential), not the total interlayer binding energy. Additionally, 'random interlayer rotations' contradicts the concept of a 'twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape,' which requires specific, well-defined twist angles.
trace.opponent_concern: The total interlayer binding energy prevents layer exfoliation but does not dictate the barrier to in-plane rotation; thus, using binding energy as the threshold for rotational stability is physically incorrect. Furthermore, a moiré potential landscape cannot be defined for a 'random' distribution of rotations.
trace.required_revision: Clarify that the thermodynamic threshold depends on the interlayer potential corrugation (rotational energy barrier) rather than total interlayer binding energy, and replace 'random interlayer rotations' with 'engineered interlayer twist angles' to maintain consistency with the moiré potential landscape.
alternative_explanations: Structural relaxation under thermal cycling could be driven by defect-mediated slip or edge effects rather than overcoming the bulk moiré rotational barrier.
Cross-plane thermal conductivity recovery might be caused by the healing of point defects or changes in interlayer spacing rather than the relaxation of the twist angle.
trace.final_scope: Van der Waals heterostructures including MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2, and graphene/hBN with engineered interlayer twist angles under sustained thermal cycling between 300 K and 500 K.

trace.target_claim: Engineered interlayer twist angles in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling if and only if the interlayer potential corrugation exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.

trace.opponent_concern: Recovery of cross-plane thermal conductivity under thermal cycling could be driven by competing mechanisms such as point defect annealing, interlayer atomic diffusion, or thermomechanical delamination, rather than solely by the rotational relaxation of the twist angle.
trace.required_revision: Explicitly bound the claim to regimes where defect generation, interlayer diffusion, and delamination are negligible, and require structural and chemical characterization to rule out these confounders when attributing conductivity changes to twist-angle relaxation.
alternative_explanations: Recovery of cross-plane thermal conductivity could be driven by point defect annealing or generation altering phonon scattering rates.
Interlayer atomic diffusion or covalent bond formation at elevated temperatures could change interfacial thermal resistance independently of twist angle.
Thermomechanical delamination or blistering due to thermal expansion mismatch could alter the effective contact area and thermal boundary resistance.

directions.title: Direct Observation of Dynamic Moiré-Phonon Scattering and Thermal Boundary Resistance Limits in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Heterostructures
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of cross-plane heat transfer in van der Waals heterostructures are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal boundary resistance, yet the dynamic coupling between twist-angle-induced strain and phonon mismatch under high-power-density operation remains unobserved. We replace the conventional static lattice mismatch model with a dynamic in-plane moiré-phonon scattering mechanism to explain thermal saturation in twisted transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures. By coupling ultrafast time-domain thermoreflectance with in-situ electron diffraction, we directly observe reversible in-plane twist-angle modulation and thermal boundary resistance evolution during thermal cycling, explicitly decoupling these effects from out-of-plane van der Waals gap expansion and defect generation. This representation shift isolates the strain-mediated in-plane phonon scattering mechanism, establishing critical binding energy thresholds for structural stability in MoS2/WS2 and extending validation to other TMDs.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Reversible in-plane twist-angle modulation during thermal cycling alters the moiré superlattice periodicity, dynamically scattering cross-plane phonons and increasing thermal boundary resistance, independent of concurrent out-of-plane van der Waals gap expansion or interfacial defect generation.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Thermal cycling induces elastic in-plane strain at the interface, which reversibly modulates the twist angle and moiré superlattice periodicity, dynamically scattering cross-plane phonons and thereby increasing thermal boundary resistance, without concurrent out-of-plane gap dilation or defect generation dominating the thermal resistance.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Direct observation of reversible in-plane twist-angle distribution changes via in-situ electron diffraction, strictly decoupled from out-of-plane lattice parameter shifts and defect density measurements, correlated with thermal boundary resistance evolution measured by time-domain thermoreflectance, contrasted against a static interface control.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Simultaneous measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity and thermal boundary resistance via time-domain thermoreflectance, and quantification of reversible in-plane twist-angle distribution via electron diffraction, strictly decoupled from out-of-plane lattice parameter shifts and defect density measurements, before and after thermal cycling, compared to a static interface control.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of reversible in-plane twist-angle distribution changes via in-situ electron diffraction, decoupled from out-of-plane expansion and defects, correlated with thermal boundary resistance evolution measured by time-domain thermoreflectance, contrasted against a static interface control ablation and validated by molecular dynamics binding energy thresholds.

assumptions: Thermal cycling within the elastic strain regime induces coherent, reversible in-plane twist-angle modulation rather than irreversible delamination, out-of-plane gap dilation, or defect generation; time-domain thermoreflectance can sufficiently resolve interfacial thermal transport from bulk degradation.

directions.title: Dynamic Stability Boundaries of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Heterostructures Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of cross-plane thermal transport in twist-angle-engineered transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures are obscured by structural instability under high power density. We replace the static equilibrium phonon transport assumption with a dynamic Moiré superlattice relaxation mechanism, revealing that excess interfacial thermal saturation beyond the intrinsic anharmonic phonon scattering baseline is bounded by a critical interfacial shear strength threshold. By coupling high-power-density thermal characterization with an adaptive thermal cycling protocol guided by in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction, we isolate the structural relaxation from chemical degradation and intrinsic Umklapp scattering limits. This representation shift from static metrology to dynamic stability validation establishes the causal link between phonon-interlayer coupling and thermal transport ceilings in nanoscale electronic systems.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Excess interfacial thermal saturation in twist-angle-engineered TMD heterostructures under high power density, beyond the intrinsic anharmonic phonon scattering (Umklapp) baseline, is governed by a critical interfacial shear strength threshold that triggers dynamic Moiré superlattice relaxation (interlayer slip), decoupling coherent phonon transport from the static twist-angle geometry.
