hypothesis.expected_mechanism: High power density drives non-equilibrium phonon populations and localized thermal heating, generating interfacial shear stress. When this thermally induced shear stress exceeds the critical interlayer shear strength (or when thermal fluctuations overcome the Moiré potential energy barrier), it triggers dynamic twist-angle relaxation (interlayer slip). This structural state change alters phonon-interlayer coupling, leading to excess interfacial thermal saturation beyond the intrinsic anharmonic phonon scattering (Umklapp) baseline.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Correlated measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity saturation and twist-angle distribution broadening via in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction during adaptive thermal cycling, explicitly isolating the excess thermal resistance beyond the intrinsic Umklapp scattering baseline and distinguishing reversible Moiré relaxation from irreversible chemical degradation.

directions.title: Closed-Loop Validation of Twist-Angle Thermal Anisotropy Stability in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides under High Power Density
directions.abstract: High-power-density heat dissipation in nanoscale devices is bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, which twist-angle engineering in 2D materials aims to tune. However, the structural stability of these twisted interfaces under extreme thermal loading remains unverified, and degradation could be confounded by point-defect generation. We establish an operando characterization framework linking in-situ nanoscale thermal observation to high-power density thermal cycling in MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides. By continuously monitoring cross-plane thermal conductivity, twist-angle distribution, and chalcogen vacancy density via electron diffraction and spectroscopy, we identify the critical thermodynamic thresholds where thermal transport saturates or degrades due to moiré reconstruction. This representation shift from static metrology to dynamic, observation-coupled thermal stressing resolves the target object and direct observation deficits, providing a definitive boundary condition for twist-engineered thermal anisotropy isolated from defect-mediated scattering.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The structural stability of the van der Waals twist-angle interface dictates the upper bound of cross-plane thermal conductivity under high power density, failing via interlayer shear sliding and moiré superlattice reconstruction when the thermally induced strain energy exceeds the interfacial binding energy, distinct from degradation caused by point-defect generation or interfacial contamination.

scientific_object.description: twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2) with controlled initial defect densities

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon transport across the moiré superlattice is highly sensitive to interlayer registry; thermal cycling induces local twist-angle fluctuations and interlayer shear sliding, which irreversibly scatters heat-carrying phonons and collapses cross-plane thermal conductivity, provided point-defect concentrations remain below the threshold for dominant vacancy-mediated scattering.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Coupling in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction, Raman thermometry, and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) as operando feedback signals to dynamically map high-power density thermal cycling limits while simultaneously monitoring chalcogen vacancy concentrations.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Phonon transport across the moiré superlattice is highly sensitive to interlayer registry; thermal cycling induces local twist-angle fluctuations and interlayer shear sliding, which irreversibly scatters heat-carrying phonons and collapses cross-plane thermal conductivity, provided point-defect concentrations remain below the threshold for dominant vacancy-mediated scattering.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Continuous operando monitoring of cross-plane thermal conductivity, twist-angle distribution, and chalcogen vacancy density during thermal cycling, compared against untwisted aligned TMD reference states and defect-engineered reference states to isolate the twist-dependent interfacial scattering mechanism from point-defect scattering.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation correlated with twist-angle distribution shifts and moiré reconstruction via electron diffraction under high heat flux, while simultaneously verifying that chalcogen vacancy densities remain below the threshold for dominant vacancy-mediated phonon scattering.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation correlated with twist-angle distribution shifts via electron diffraction under high heat flux, validated against molecular dynamics predictions of critical binding energy and controlled for point-defect concentrations.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The critical thermodynamic threshold where thermally induced strain energy exceeds the interfacial binding energy, causing irreversible moiré superlattice reconstruction and thermal conductivity collapse, provided this occurs prior to or independently of catastrophic point-defect accumulation or chemical desorption.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Limits of heat transfer in twisted 2D material interfaces under high power density, specifically bounding the thermal transport limit via the structural stability of the moiré superlattice against thermally induced strain and interlayer shear, explicitly isolated from point-defect and contamination-mediated scattering.
assumptions: Molecular dynamics predictions of critical binding energy thresholds are transferable to experimental nanoscale thermal cycling; in-situ electron diffraction and spectroscopy can resolve twist-angle fluctuations and point-defect densities at relevant timescales without beam-induced artifacts confounding the measurements.

directions.falsifier: Evidence that cross-plane thermal conductivity collapse under high power density occurs without concurrent twist-angle fluctuations or interlayer shear, or evidence that the collapse is fully accounted for by a concurrent increase in point-defect density (e.g., chalcogen vacancies) or interfacial contamination, indicating an alternative degradation mechanism.
directions.gap_alignment: The intervention directly targets the unmapped target object by defining the twisted TMD interface as the physical system under thermomechanical stress, and resolves the direct observation deficit by using in-situ electron diffraction, Raman thermometry, and spectroscopy as the operando feedback signal to distinguish structural reconstruction from defect generation.

trace.target_claim: The structural stability of the van der Waals twist-angle interface dictates the upper bound of cross-plane thermal conductivity under high power density, failing via interfacial slipping when thermal stress exceeds the critical binding energy.
trace.scientific_concern: The term 'interfacial slipping' is colloquial and 'thermal stress exceeds critical binding energy' conflates mechanical stress (force/area) with thermodynamic binding energy (energy/area). Additionally, 'closed-loop' may overstate the characterization framework if it merely monitors rather than actively controls the thermal load based on real-time feedback.
trace.opponent_concern: Thermal expansion mismatch in van der Waals heterostructures primarily induces in-plane strain rather than pure shear; thus, the failure mode might be moiré superlattice reconstruction or domain wall formation rather than simple interlayer sliding.
trace.required_revision: Replace 'interfacial slipping' with 'interlayer shear sliding and moiré superlattice reconstruction'. Correct the boundary condition to state failure occurs when 'thermally induced strain energy exceeds the interfacial binding energy'. Clarify 'closed-loop' as 'operando' to align with standard materials science metrology.
alternative_explanations: Thermal degradation of cross-plane conductivity may be driven by the formation of interfacial vacancies or chalcogen desorption under high heat flux, rather than purely mechanical interlayer sliding.
trace.final_scope: Limits of heat transfer in twisted 2D material interfaces under high power density, specifically bounding the thermal transport limit via the structural stability of the moiré superlattice against thermally induced strain and interlayer shear.

directions.title: Direct Observation and Closed-Loop Engineering of Non-Equilibrium Hot Optical Phonon Scattering at Epitaxial Interfaces via Ultrafast Electron Diffraction
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing non-equilibrium phonon scattering remain obscured by steady-state measurements and confounded by bulk thermalization. We introduce a representation shift from steady-state thermal diffusion to ultrafast transient dynamics, using momentum-resolved ultrafast electron diffraction (UED) to directly characterize hot optical phonon populations at GaN/AlN epitaxial thin-film interfaces. By decoupling optical phonons from coherent strain pulses and bounding pump fluence to isolate interfacial scattering from bulk electron-phonon thermalization, we iteratively perturb the interfacial structure via sub-monolayer ion-beam mixing. This isolates the specific non-equilibrium phonon scattering mechanisms that dictate thermal transport limits, providing the missing direct observation of interfacial thermal dynamics and establishing a new paradigm for precision thermal metrology.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering at GaN/AlN epitaxial interfaces is governed by atomic-scale bonding defect states. By employing momentum-resolved ultrafast electron diffraction to decouple optical phonons from coherent strain pulses and bounding pump fluence to isolate interfacial scattering from bulk electron-phonon thermalization, this mechanism can be directly characterized and iteratively perturbed via sub-monolayer ion-beam mixing to modulate interfacial thermal resistance.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Iteratively altering the interfacial composition via sub-monolayer ion-beam mixing perturbs the local defect density and bond stiffness, which modulates the non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering rates at the interface. This structural perturbation reduces the interfacial thermal resistance until bounded by the fundamental thermal saturation limit, distinct from bulk electron-phonon thermalization limits.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparing the momentum-resolved transient hot optical phonon population decay rates characterized via ultrafast electron diffraction between the iteratively perturbed interfaces and the unengineered baseline, specifically isolating the interfacial phonon transmission bottleneck from bulk decay and coherent strain signals.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct momentum-resolved characterization of transient hot optical phonon populations via ultrafast electron diffraction, contrasted against the unengineered baseline interface, and bounded by the high power density optical pump condition to exclude bulk electron-phonon thermalization.

hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The high power density optical pump defines the boundary condition where pump fluence induces irreversible non-thermal melting, deep-level defect generation, or overwhelms the UED signal with bulk electron-phonon thermalization, decoupling the reversible interfacial phonon scattering mechanism from structural degradation or bulk confounders.

directions.title: Spectrally-Resolved Inelastic Hot Phonon Coupling at Metal-Dielectric Interfaces Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: Interfacial thermal resistance in nanoscale devices is conventionally modeled using elastic diffuse phonon scattering, which fails to capture non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations under high power density. We introduce an inelastic hot phonon coupling mechanism at metal-dielectric interfaces, demonstrating that atomic-scale bonding modifications enable inelastic phonon-phonon scattering channels that fundamentally alter spectral thermal transport. By employing time-domain thermoreflectance with low-fluence pump suppression ablation and spectrally resolved probing, we isolate the inelastic contribution from classical temperature-dependent thermal transport. Crucially, we rigorously decouple this interfacial bottleneck from measurement artifacts like non-linear thermoreflectance and bulk anharmonic scattering. This representation shift from elastic to inelastic scattering exposes the invariant relationship between interfacial bond stiffness and hot phonon generation, resolving the missing phenomenon in atomic-scale thermal metrology.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The interfacial thermal resistance under high power density is fundamentally limited by an inelastic hot phonon bottleneck at the metal-dielectric interface, which scales non-linearly with pump fluence due to non-equilibrium optical phonon populations, distinct from classical temperature-dependent thermal transport and non-linear measurement artifacts.

scientific_object.description: metal_dielectric_interface_system

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: Atomic-scale bonding variations at the interface alter the phonon density of states overlap and anharmonic coupling strength. Under high power density, this enables inelastic scattering channels that generate a non-equilibrium hot optical phonon population, creating a thermal bottleneck that is distinct from the classical temperature-dependent reduction in thermal conductivity and independent of bulk anharmonic scattering limits.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Replacing the elastic diffuse phonon scattering model with the inelastic hot phonon coupling mechanism, applying interfacial bonding modification to tune the atomic-scale bonding stiffness, and implementing rigorous calibration protocols to bound non-linear thermoreflectance and bulk anharmonic scattering.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Atomic-scale bonding variations alter phonon DOS overlap and anharmonic coupling, enabling inelastic scattering channels that generate hot optical phonons. This modifies the spectral energy distribution and increases the effective interfacial thermal resistance under high power density, independent of the bulk temperature-dependent thermal conductivity and non-linear thermoreflectance effects.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The deviation of interfacial thermal resistance from linear fluence scaling in time-domain thermoreflectance measurements, specifically isolated via low-fluence pump suppression ablation, spectrally resolved probing, and rigorous calibration of non-linear thermoreflectance coefficients and bulk anharmonic scattering to definitively rule out these confounders.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of non-linear interfacial thermal resistance scaling with pump fluence in time-domain thermoreflectance that persists after rigorous calibration of non-linear thermoreflectance coefficients and subtraction of bulk anharmonic scattering contributions, confirming the presence of the hot phonon bottleneck.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of non-linear interfacial thermal resistance scaling with pump fluence in time-domain thermoreflectance, contrasting with linear elastic model predictions, classical temperature-dependent models, and bounded measurement artifacts.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails or becomes negligible when the dielectric layer is amorphous, when the optical phonon lifetime is comparable to or shorter than the acoustic phonon transit time, when the non-linearity can be fully explained by bulk temperature-dependent thermal conductivity, or when the observed non-linearity is entirely accounted for by non-linear thermoreflectance or bulk anharmonic scattering.

directions.title: Feedback-Controlled Thermal Saturation: Closing the Loop Between Precision Thermal Metrology and Adaptive Electrical Pumping to Reveal Hot Optical Phonon Limits in Graphene-Silicon Carbide Heterojunctions
directions.abstract: The fundamental thermal saturation limit of nanoscale electronic interfaces under high power density is governed by non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering, but remains obscured when measurements are decoupled from process control. We close this gap by implementing a feedback loop between precision thermal metrology and adaptive electrical pumping, transforming the monolayer graphene-4H-silicon carbide heterojunction into a dynamically controlled target object. The feedback signal—interfacial thermal resistance trajectory—drives bounded updates to pulse width, duty cycle, and peak power density to establish the macroscopic thermal saturation ceiling. To isolate the specific contribution of hot optical phonon accumulation to this ceiling, we employ isotopic perturbation (12C vs 13C graphene) and decouple its effect on the full phonon spectrum by comparing the macroscopic saturation trajectory against the theoretically bounded acoustic phonon transport limit. This representation shift resolves the unmapped target object gap and provides a falsifiable framework for ultimate heat dissipation limits.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The macroscopic thermal saturation ceiling of the graphene-SiC heterojunction under high power density is dynamically bounded by closing the loop between interfacial thermal resistance metrology and adaptive electrical pumping, while the specific contribution of non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering to this ceiling is isolated through isotopic perturbation of the graphene lattice, explicitly decoupled from the concurrent reduction in acoustic phonon transport caused by isotopic mass disorder.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Rewiring precision thermal metrology feedback to drive bounded updates in the adaptive electrical pumping protocol to establish the macroscopic thermal saturation boundary, combined with isotopic perturbation and theoretical decoupling of acoustic phonon mass-disorder scattering to isolate the hot optical phonon mechanism.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: The closed-loop control establishes the maximum sustainable power density before thermal runaway, while isotopic perturbation shifts the full phonon spectrum; isolating the hot phonon bottleneck requires explicitly bounding and subtracting the concurrent degradation of acoustic phonon mean free paths caused by isotopic mass disorder.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The divergence in the macroscopic thermal saturation trajectories (maximum sustainable power density) between natural 12C and 13C-enriched graphene under closed-loop adaptive pumping, after explicitly subtracting the theoretically bounded contribution of acoustic phonon mass-disorder scattering, isolating the specific contribution of hot optical phonon scattering to the thermal resistance ceiling.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Measurement of macroscopic thermal saturation trajectories under closed-loop adaptive pumping, contrasted across isotopic perturbations and explicitly decoupled from the theoretically bounded acoustic phonon transport limit to isolate the hot optical phonon contribution, bounded by the identification of an irreversible thermal failure threshold.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct observation of thermal transport limits in nanoscale devices: while advanced materials like graphene offer superior intrinsic thermal conductivity, their practical heat dissipation is fundamentally bottlenecked by interface thermal boundary resistance, and classical drift-diffusion models significantly underestimate peak temperatures by failing to account for non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations and isotopic mass-disorder scattering.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The absolute peak power density threshold where the adaptive electrical pumping protocol can no longer suppress thermal runaway, resulting in irreversible interfacial degradation, or the point where isotopic mass disorder degrades acoustic transport so severely that the optical phonon bottleneck becomes indistinguishable from the acoustic floor.

directions.title: Mode-Resolved Non-Equilibrium Phonon Transmission at Carbon Nanotube-Silicon Interfaces: Resolving the Boundary Variable in High-Power-Density Thermal Transport
directions.abstract: Classical drift-diffusion models fail to capture heat dissipation limits in nanoscale devices because they treat interfaces as equilibrium thermal resistances, ignoring non-equilibrium hot phonon populations. We introduce a mode-resolved, non-equilibrium phonon transmission boundary condition to replace the classical Kapitza resistance model. By manipulating interfacial covalent bridging density in vertically aligned carbon nanotube arrays on silicon substrates, we demonstrate that hot optical phonon hybridization dictates the true thermal transport limit, provided bulk anharmonic decay and electron-phonon coupling are sub-dominant. Using ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy coupled with frequency-domain thermoreflectance, we resolve the phonon mean free path and validate the spectral overlap mechanism while explicitly decoupling electronic contributions. This representation shift from continuum resistance to spectrally resolved transmission establishes the precise boundary conditions where interfacial resistance overtakes bulk conduction under high power densities.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The fundamental limit of interfacial thermal transport under high power density is dictated by the spectral hybridization and transmission probability of non-equilibrium hot optical phonons across the covalently bridged interface, contingent upon the interfacial transmission rate exceeding the rates of bulk anharmonic decay and electron-phonon coupling.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Replace the classical equilibrium thermal boundary resistance with a spectrally resolved, non-equilibrium phonon transmission boundary condition, and manipulate the interfacial covalent bridging density via controlled Ti adhesion layers while maintaining regimes where bulk scattering is sub-dominant.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Increasing covalent bridging density enhances the spectral overlap between CNT optical phonons and Si acoustic phonons, facilitating resonant hot phonon transmission and shifting the bottleneck from interfacial scattering to bulk non-equilibrium phonon decay, assuming electron-phonon coupling remains weak.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy reveals a divergence in hot optical phonon decay rates between classical model predictions and the mode-resolved transmission model, specifically at power densities where non-equilibrium populations dominate, and this divergence scales with interfacial bridging density but remains invariant when electron-phonon coupling is artificially enhanced (e.g., via heavy doping).
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Quantitative comparison of effective thermal boundary conductance and hot phonon decay rates measured via FDTR and ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy against the predictions of the mode-resolved transmission matrix and classical drift-diffusion models, including controls to verify that electron-phonon coupling does not dominate the transient decay.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy and frequency-domain thermoreflectance measurements of VACNT-Si interfaces with controlled Ti adhesion layers, compared against classical drift-diffusion and mode-resolved transmission models, with explicit decoupling of electronic and bulk scattering contributions.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mode-resolved transmission model fails and reverts to classical Kapitza behavior or bulk-limited behavior when the interfacial bridging density is too low, when the power density is insufficient to generate a non-equilibrium hot phonon population, or when electron-phonon coupling and bulk anharmonic decay rates exceed the interfacial transmission rate.

Ultrafast transient absorption and FDTR measurements can cleanly decouple interfacial hot phonon decay dynamics from bulk thermal transport and electronic contributions.

directions.title: Stability-Bounded Dynamic Moiré Potential Modulation for Cross-Plane Thermal Conductivity Tuning in Twisted van der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: Quasi-static modulation of the moiré interlayer registry via applied mechanical strain tunes cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted van der Waals heterostructures. However, idealized models suffer from measurement construct mismatch by conflating moiré-driven interfacial coupling changes with structural degradation like interlayer slip. We introduce a stability-bounded moiré registry modulation mechanism that identifies critical interlayer binding energy thresholds. By correlating strain-induced thermal conductivity variations with structural tracking, we isolate true moiré-mediated interfacial thermal transport from structural relaxation, establishing a rigorous boundary condition for adaptive thermal management in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted van der Waals heterostructures can be quasi-statically and reversibly tuned via applied mechanical strain through moiré-modulated interlayer registry, provided the applied strain remains below the critical interlayer binding energy threshold that triggers structural relaxation.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Apply controlled quasi-static biaxial strain (0-2%) to twisted TMD heterostructures to alter the moiré interlayer registry, bounded by critical interlayer binding energy thresholds.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: The applied strain alters the moiré periodicity and local interlayer atomic registry, which modifies the interfacial van der Waals coupling and cross-plane phonon transmission pathways, thereby tuning the cross-plane thermal conductivity without inducing interlayer slip or twist-angle drift.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The reversibility and absence of hysteresis in cross-plane thermal conductivity during quasi-static strain cycling, contrasted with the structural stability (constant twist-angle distribution) measured via UED and Raman spectroscopy, distinguishing moiré-mediated interfacial transport from irreversible structural degradation.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity hysteresis during quasi-static strain cycling, correlated with quantitative twist-angle distribution maps from UED and strain profiles from micro-Raman, to prove that thermal tuning is strictly bounded by the structural stability limit.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Reversible cross-plane thermal conductivity tuning correlated with invariant twist-angle distributions under quasi-static strain, validated against molecular dynamics predictions of moiré-modulated interfacial coupling.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails and the claim becomes invalid when the applied strain exceeds the critical interlayer binding energy threshold, leading to irreversible interlayer slip, twist-angle drift, or fracture, which manifests as hysteresis or permanent shifts in thermal conductivity.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures under quasi-static biaxial strain below the critical interlayer binding energy threshold.

trace.scientific_concern: The term 'moiré potential modulation' typically describes in-plane electronic or phononic band structure effects. For cross-plane thermal conductivity, the relevant mechanism is the modulation of interlayer registry and van der Waals coupling across the moiré superlattice. trace.opponent_concern: Cross-plane thermal transport is dominated by interfacial Kapitza resistance. Strain-induced changes in cross-plane thermal conductivity might be conflated with strain-induced changes in bulk phonon dispersion or contact resistance, rather than purely moiré-modulated interlayer coupling.
trace.required_revision: Reframe 'moiré potential modulation' to 'moiré-modulated interlayer registry' for cross-plane transport. alternative_explanations: Observed changes in cross-plane thermal conductivity under strain may be primarily due to strain-induced modifications of the bulk out-of-plane phonon dispersion or changes in thermal contact resistance at the metal-TMD interface, rather than moiré-modulated interlayer coupling.

directions.title: Time-Temperature-Transformation Stability Diagrams for Twist-Angle Engineering in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal transport in van der Waals heterostructures assumes structural stability of the moiré configuration under thermal load, but this assumption lacks a predictive stability boundary. We apply time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram methodology as a phenomenological framework to map the critical temperature-time combinations where twist angles remain fixed versus undergo interfacial rotational relaxation in MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures. By systematically annealing heterostructures across isothermal conditions and quantifying twist angle distributions via selected area electron diffraction alongside cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements, we construct a stability phase diagram. We test the hypothesis that if relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, it will trace a characteristic nose curve where thermal activation of rotational relaxation is fastest. This provides a predictive framework for operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport, linking structural relaxation kinetics to moiré-periodicity-dependent phonon scattering.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The twist_angle_stability_state in transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures follows time-temperature-transformation kinetics if interfacial rotational relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, exhibiting a characteristic nose curve in temperature-time space, such that cross-plane thermal conductivity varies predictably according to moiré superlattice periodicity and phonon scattering regimes when the twist angle exceeds a critical relaxation threshold.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Systematic isothermal annealing of twisted_vdw_heterostructures across a temperature-time matrix (150°C–500°C, 1 min–100 hrs) to perturb the twist_angle_stability_state and activate interfacial_rotational_relaxation, with characterization before and after to construct the phenomenological stability_phase_diagram.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: If rotational relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, the competition between domain nucleation rate and growth rate (limited by interfacial phonon drag at high T) will produce a TTT nose curve. Cross-plane thermal conductivity will vary non-monotonously based on the resulting moiré superlattice periodicity and associated phonon scattering regimes, rather than a simple monotonic degradation.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The stability phase diagram must exhibit a nose curve shape, distinguishing it from simple Arrhenius relaxation. The twist angle distribution must correlate with cross-plane thermal conductivity variations that align with moiré superlattice phonon scattering models, rather than a simple monotonic degradation or defect-dominated changes.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Selected area electron diffraction to distinguish between uniform rotation and domain nucleation/growth; cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements correlated with moiré periodicity; validation of the nose curve shape in temperature-time space.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Selected area electron diffraction patterns across temperature-time matrix; time-domain thermoreflectance cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements; molecular dynamics for moiré phonon scattering and activation barriers.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The TTT stability framework fails if: (1) relaxation follows simple monotonic Arrhenius kinetics without a nose curve; (2) thermal conductivity changes do not correlate with moiré periodicity models; (3) relaxation is dominated by uniform sliding rather than domain nucleation and growth; (4) the framework does not transfer to other TMD combinations.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Valid for transition metal dichalcogenide twisted bilayer heterostructures with twist angles 0°–5° under isothermal annealing conditions 150°C–500°C; provides a phenomenological stability boundary for twist-angle-engineered cross-plane thermal transport, contingent on the observation of distinct domain nucleation and growth kinetics.

directions.gap_alignment: Addresses the gap by providing a phenomenological predictive boundary for the operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport in nanoscale devices, linking structural relaxation kinetics to fundamental thermal transport limits.

assumptions: Interface transmission probability can be parameterized by a single effective bonding energy metric
Bulk phonon mean free path distribution remains invariant under moderate power density increases
Non-equilibrium optical phonon populations do not significantly alter interface transmission coefficients
The crossover threshold is material-pair specific but follows predictable scaling laws
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

directions.title: Quantitative Boundary Conditions for the Maximum Transmission Limit Model at Weakly Bonded Interfaces Under High Power Density
directions.abstract: The maximum transmission limit model reliably predicts thermal conductance for clean, strongly bonded interfaces but fails for weakly bonded or contaminated junctions. We establish the critical effective interfacial phonon transmission coefficient as the boundary variable where interfacial Kapitza resistance overtakes bulk resistance, scaling with the bulk phonon mean free path ratio. By replacing the equilibrium Kapitza transport model with a non-equilibrium phonon population mechanism, we define the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit. Under high-power-density excitation, non-equilibrium phonon populations shift this transmission threshold, revealing the transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance and bounding the model's predictive applicability, provided irreversible structural degradation is excluded.

mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

directions.title: Discriminating Phonon and Electron Heat Conduction in High-Power-Density Materials via Carrier Density Variation and Spectral Phonon Imaging
directions.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials remain obscured by aggregate thermal measurements. We introduce a discriminating observation protocol that replaces unpartitioned thermal transport assumptions with controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, exploiting the differential scaling of electron and phonon conductivities. By coupling this perturbation with spectral phonon imaging to directly visualize phonon mean free paths and scattering rates, we isolate the phonon-limited regime from the electron-limited regime. This mechanism-commit innovation resolves the identifiability gap in high-power-density thermal transport, establishing explicit validity boundaries for the Wiedemann-Franz law under extreme carrier injection and defining the fundamental limits of heat dissipation.

assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

directions.title: Moiré Potential Energy Barrier Threshold Governs Rotational Stability in Twisted Van Der Waals Heterostructures Under Thermal Cycling
directions.abstract: Random interlayer rotations suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures, but their persistence under operational thermal cycling remains unverified beyond MoS2 and WS2. We propose that rotational stability is governed by a critical threshold: the interlayer binding energy must exceed the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential barrier to prevent thermal-activation-driven relaxation. We synthesize twisted heterostructures of MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 with controlled random rotations and subject them to controlled versus open-loop thermal cycling. Cross-plane thermal conductivity evolution, measured via time-domain thermoreflectance, serves as a structural proxy for rotational relaxation. Correlated moiré superlattice imaging distinguishes rotational relaxation from other degradation mechanisms, establishing material-dependent stability boundaries and identifying failure regimes where binding energy falls below the critical moiré potential threshold.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Rotational stability of engineered random interlayer rotations in van der Waals heterostructures under thermal cycling is governed by a critical threshold where the interlayer binding energy must exceed the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential barrier to prevent thermal-activation-driven relaxation.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Substituting the unconstrained rotational persistence assumption with the moiré potential energy barrier threshold mechanism, and introducing an open-loop thermal cycling comparator ablation to isolate the threshold mechanism's contribution.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: When thermal activation energy exceeds the moiré potential barrier, rotational relaxation occurs, recovering cross-plane thermal conductivity; when bounded below the barrier, the engineered anisotropy persists.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Divergent evolution of cross-plane thermal conductivity (measured via TDTR) and moiré superlattice degradation (via STEM) between controlled threshold-bounded cycling and open-loop cycling across MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Divergent evolution of cross-plane thermal conductivity and moiré superlattice degradation between controlled threshold-bounded cycling and open-loop cycling, establishing material-dependent stability boundaries.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Comparative TDTR and STEM measurements of cross-plane thermal conductivity and moiré superlattice integrity under controlled versus open-loop thermal cycling protocols.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails or becomes inaccessible when the moiré potential energy landscape is too shallow (e.g., WSe2/MoSe2 at large twist angles) or when thermal cycling induces irreversible structural damage (cracking, delamination) rather than pure rotational relaxation.

directions.title: Bounding Reversible Moiré Phonon Scattering Limits in Twist-Engineered TMDs via Sequential Thermal Cycling and Binding Energy Thresholds
directions.abstract: High-power-density heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics is bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy under extreme thermal loads remains unverified due to the confounding effects of irreversible defect generation during thermal stress. We propose a sequential verification-reversal approach to back-infer the mechanism of cross-plane thermal transport collapse in MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). By decoupling time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) into pre- and post-thermal cycling measurements, we isolate the reversible structural drift of the moiré superlattice from irreversible damage. This feedback loop, calibrated against molecular dynamics predictions of critical interlayer binding energy, bounds the critical heat flux where engineered anisotropy fails, establishing the true structural stability boundary for nanoscale thermal management.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The collapse of cross-plane thermal transport in twist-engineered TMDs under high power density is bounded by a reversible moiré superlattice decoherence threshold dictated by interlayer binding energy, distinguishable from irreversible defect generation.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Thermal stress induces reversible moiré periodicity degradation when the local heat flux exceeds the interlayer binding energy threshold, altering phonon scattering and collapsing thermal anisotropy before irreversible defect generation occurs.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Correlation between the experimentally measured critical heat flux for thermal conductivity collapse and the molecular dynamics predicted binding energy thresholds across different TMD material pairs (MoS2/WS2 vs. MoSe2/WSe2).

hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds only when the applied thermal cycling remains below the threshold for irreversible defect generation or interlayer delamination; beyond this boundary, the mechanism shifts from reversible moiré decoherence to permanent structural damage.

directions.title: Validation of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy Limits in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides via Closed-Loop Thermal Cycling
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of cross-plane thermal transport in twist-angle-engineered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) under high power density are constrained by interfacial structural stability. We replace the assumption of static moiré phonon scattering with a critical binding energy threshold-governed interfacial slip mechanism. By iteratively measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity and quantifying twist-angle distribution via electron diffraction during thermal cycling, we back-infer the binding energy thresholds governing phonon scattering in MoS2/WS2 and extended TMDs. An open-loop thermal cycling control ablation isolates the mechanical slip mechanism from chemical degradation, defining the fundamental thermal transport limit and stability boundary for moiré-engineered interfaces.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in transition metal dichalcogenides under high power density is bounded by a critical interfacial binding energy threshold that triggers thermally activated moiré lattice slip, which can be empirically validated by closing the loop between interfacial thermal resistance characterization and thermal cycling boundary conditions.

The closed-loop feedback ensures the thermal cycling process precisely targets this slip threshold without confounding chemical degradation.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Ablating the feedback loop using open-loop thermal cycling control will show that open-loop cycling induces irreversible chemical degradation (e.g., chalcogen vacancies) rather than purely mechanical twist-angle relaxation, whereas the closed-loop isolates the mechanical slip mechanism.

Here, we replace the static twist-angle phonon scattering model with a thermally-induced twist-angle relaxation mechanism to explain thermal transport degradation under high power density. By correlating cross-plane time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with electron diffraction quantification before and after thermal cycling, we directly observe the structural relaxation of MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides. A thermal cycling ablation protocol isolates the contribution of twist-angle distribution perturbations from intrinsic phonon scattering, establishing critical binding energy thresholds where engineered thermal anisotropy fails.

directions.title: Direct Observation of Saturating Interfacial Thermal Conductance in Annealed Graphene/SiO2 Heterostructures Reveals Bonding-Dependent Phonon Transmission Limits
directions.abstract: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance fundamentally limits heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing thermal conductance saturation remain unobserved. We demonstrate that interfacial thermal conductance in graphene/SiO2 heterostructures saturates at a critical covalent bond density, revealing a fundamental limit to phonon transmission enhancement through interface engineering. Using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy, we directly observe non-monotonic thermal conductance evolution during controlled annealing, where initial van der Waals-to-covalent bonding transitions increase conductance, but excessive covalent bonding introduces defect scattering that degrades heat transfer. This discriminating observation falsifies monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a bonding-configuration-dependent upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Interfacial thermal conductance in graphene/SiO2 heterostructures exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on covalent bond density, saturating and degrading at high defect concentrations due to competing phonon transmission enhancement and defect-induced scattering.

scientific_object.target_object: graphene/SiO2 van der Waals heterostructure interface

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Initial van der Waals-to-covalent bonding transitions enhance phonon transmission across the interface, increasing thermal conductance. However, excessive covalent bonding introduces defect scattering and interfacial roughness, which degrade phonon mean free path and reduce thermal conductance, establishing a saturation limit.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Direct measurement of a non-monotonic thermal conductance curve as a function of annealing temperature and covalent bond density, where conductance peaks at an intermediate bonding state and degrades upon over-annealing, falsifying monotonic bonding-conductance models.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of thermal conductance saturation and degradation correlated with quantitative measurements of covalent bond density and defect concentration across a controlled annealing series, isolated from bulk property changes.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Direct experimental observation of thermal conductance saturation at atomic-scale interfaces using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy correlated with atomic bonding configuration.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The non-monotonic mechanism holds for annealing temperatures up to 600°C where graphene remains intact; beyond this, bulk graphene degradation or SiO2 phase changes confound the interfacial thermal transport measurements.

assumptions: Thermal annealing primarily modifies the interfacial bonding configuration without altering the bulk thermal properties of the graphene and SiO2 layers up to 600°C.

directions.title: Feedback-Optimized Covalent Bridge Phonon Coupling at Graphene-Diamond Heterointerfaces: Bounding the Fundamental Interfacial Thermal Transport Limit
directions.abstract: High-power-density heat dissipation in nanoscale devices is bottlenecked by interfacial thermal boundary resistance rather than intrinsic material conductivity. We address the unmapped phenomenon of atomic-scale thermal saturation at heterointerfaces by implementing a characterization-feedback loop that iteratively tunes covalent bridge density via controlled ion-beam irradiation. Using frequency-domain thermoreflectance as the feedback signal, we update irradiation dose conditions to minimize thermal boundary resistance at graphene-diamond heterointerfaces. Temperature-dependent defect density ablations isolate the covalent bridge resonant phonon coupling mechanism from point-defect scattering, while high-power-density stress tests bound the failure threshold where anharmonic phonon scattering or irreversible structural degradation dominates. This establishes the fundamental phonon transport limit at atomically engineered heterointerfaces under operational heat flux conditions.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Covalent bridge resonant phonon coupling, tunable via characterization-feedback-guided ion-beam irradiation, governs the fundamental thermal boundary resistance at graphene-diamond heterointerfaces under high power density, replacing the diffuse acoustic mismatch model as the dominant interfacial phonon transport mechanism.

hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: Under high power density stress testing (>1 GW/m^2 heat flux), the covalent bridge mechanism fails when anharmonic three-phonon scattering or irreversible structural degradation (bridge breaking, graphitization) causes thermal boundary resistance to increase despite maintained covalent bonding, defining the fundamental operational limit.

directions.title: Decoupling Interfacial Phonon Scattering from Thermal Boundary Resistance via Static Twist-Angle Modulation in van der Waals Heterostructures
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat transfer in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the precise role of atomic-scale bonding in dictating phonon scattering remains unresolved due to reliance on the generic diffuse acoustic mismatch assumption. We propose a structure-property-mechanism study on van der Waals heterostructures to isolate the contribution of bonding-dependent interfacial phonon scattering to thermal boundary resistance. By synthesizing a static twist-angle library, we systematically alter the atomic bonding and structural state at the interface without dynamic modulation artifacts. Using time-domain thermoreflectance with optimized sub-nanometer thermal penetration depths, we ablate the twist-angle-dependent bonding states to directly observe the mechanism's impact on heat dissipation. This approach establishes the fundamental material-dependent limits of thermal transport at pristine atomic interfaces, replacing weak scattering assumptions with a refined, bonding-dependent mechanism.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Interfacial thermal resistance in van der Waals heterostructures is strictly governed by a bonding-dependent interfacial phonon scattering mechanism rather than the generic diffuse acoustic mismatch assumption.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Synthesize a static twist-angle library of van der Waals heterostructures to systematically alter the atomic bonding and structural state at the interface.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Variations in the twist angle modulate the interfacial van der Waals coupling and phonon density of states overlap, directly dictating the rate of interfacial phonon scattering and thereby bounding the thermal boundary resistance.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Time-domain thermoreflectance measurements across the static twist-angle library will show distinct deviations in interfacial thermal resistance that correlate with the twist-angle-dependent bonding states, falsifying the uniform predictions of the diffuse acoustic mismatch model.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Precision time-domain thermoreflectance characterization of interfacial thermal resistance across the static twist-angle library, compared against theoretical predictions of both the diffuse acoustic mismatch model and the bonding-dependent phonon scattering mechanism.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Precision time-domain thermoreflectance characterization of interfacial thermal resistance across the static twist-angle library, compared against theoretical predictions of both the diffuse acoustic mismatch model and the bonding-dependent phonon scattering mechanism.

directions.title: Back-Inferring the Spectrally Resolved Interfacial Phonon Transmission Coefficient via Closed-Loop Mean Free Path Spectroscopy and Interfacial Perturbation
directions.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoelectronics are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet isolating the exact boundary variable governing phonon scattering remains unresolved. We introduce a closed-loop experimental framework that uses spectrally resolved phonon mean free path distributions, extracted via broadband transient thermal grating spectroscopy, as a feedback signal to iteratively perturb the interfacial boundary condition. By systematically tuning the substrate coupling in graphene heterostructures and comparing the extracted accumulation functions against a spectrally resolved kinetic transport model, we back-infer the dominant kinetic transport scattering mechanism. This approach resolves the unmapped boundary variable by decoupling diffuse interfacial scattering from intrinsic anharmonic decay, establishing the precise geometric and material thresholds where Kapitza resistance overtakes bulk resistance.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The spectrally resolved interfacial phonon transmission coefficient acts as the fundamental boundary variable that dictates the crossover from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal transport, and can be uniquely back-inferred by closing the loop between mean-free-path-resolved spectroscopy and controlled interfacial perturbations.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Iteratively perturbing the interfacial coupling (e.g., via controlled thermal annealing or electrostatic gating) on a single heterostructure while using the extracted phonon mean free path distribution as a feedback signal to constrain a spectrally resolved kinetic transport model.

hypothesis.discriminating_observation: The convergence of the back-inferred spectrally resolved transmission coefficient across iterative perturbations, which correctly predicts the threshold where Kapitza resistance overtakes bulk resistance, contrasted against the failure of ablated model branches (e.g., specular scattering assumptions) to fit the feedback signal.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: The observation of a convergent spectrally resolved interfacial phonon transmission coefficient across iteratively perturbed boundary conditions, contrasted against ablated model branches, demonstrating that the extracted boundary variable uniquely predicts the crossover threshold where interfacial thermal resistance overtakes bulk thermal resistance.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Broadband transient thermal grating spectroscopy measurements of the thermal conductivity accumulation function across systematically annealed graphene heterostructures, compared against spectrally resolved kinetic transport models with ablated scattering mechanisms.
